Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-102 and consent of Instructor
Notes: One-quarter course credit. Offered satisfactory/unsatisfactory. May be repeated. Students may count up to one credit from courses numbered 290-298 toward graduation.

Course Description: Practicum in which students gain real-world software engineering experience by maintaining, updating, and implementing features into existing software projects for on-campus clients. Students receive guidance during frequent stand-up meetings, give progress updates through regular presentations, and reflect on their experience using new tools and software engineering practices. Depending on the semester and projects available, students may work in teams or individually. Enrollment will vary from semester to semester based on current client needs. Students should reach out to the instructor to discuss availability of projects and anticipated availability of spots in the practicum.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any 200-level computer science course and consent of the instructor
Notes: May be repeated for credit with permission of the department, but does not count toward concentration requirements.

Course Description: Independent work on a research project under supervision of a faculty member.
Prerequisite Narrative: Consent of Instructor
Notes: Students may repeat 298 for credit, but only a maximum of one credit of Computer Science Research can count towards satisfying the requirements for departmental honors.

Course Description: This course discusses deep learning, covering foundational machine learning principles (loss functions, bias-variance trade-off, and optimization) and advanced models (Multilayer Perceptron, Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Transformers). The course is project-based, emphasizing the application of these techniques to real-world datasets using the deep learning framework PyTorch.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220, MATH-224

Course Description: Introduction to the development of robotic systems for the space environment. Students will develop software for an autonomous lunar rover. Students will learn Robot Operating System One (ROS1), ROS Visualization (RViz), and Gazebo Simulator. Topics include sensing, mapping, navigation, path planning, and multi-robot coordination. Programming intensive.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220, CPSCI-230, or CPSCI-240; and MATH-224; and MATH-216; and MATH-254; or permission of instructor.
Prerequisites: CPSCI-220, , CPSCI-230, , CPSCI-240, , MATH 224, , MATH 216, , MATH-254,

Course Description: Study of how computers are built. Starting with fundamental logic gates, students will learn how to construct fundamental computational, memory and control components using digital logic. Students study the implementation of arithmetic logic units, processor control and datapath design. Topics will include performance analysis, pipelining, cache design, virtual memory, disk storage, and multicore design. Theory intensive.

A discussion of modern algorithms and advanced techniques, with analysis of time and space complexity in theory and practice. Topics will include, among others: geometric algorithms, graph algorithms, hashing, parallel algorithms, external memory algorithms, parameterized algorithms, and techniques for solving NP-hard problems in practice.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-230

Course Description: Study of the design and implementation of computer operating systems. Students will develop at least four significant projects related to the topics of process scheduling, interprocess communication, memory management, file systems, access control, device drivers and security. Programming intensive.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-240

Course Description: Introduction to access technology and the development of accessible systems. In this course, students build and evaluate various access technologies. This course teaches students the deep inner workings of today’s user interface technology and serves as a guide for building the user interfaces of the future. Topics include: text-to-speech, speech recognition, screen readers, screen magnification, alternative input, tactile displays, and web transformation. Programming intensive.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220

Course Description: This course covers deep learning fundamentals, from core machine learning concepts (e.g.: loss functions, bias-variance, and optimization) to advanced models like Multilayer Perceptrons, Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, and Transformers. Students will gain hands-on experience by applying these techniques to real-world datasets using various deep learning frameworks.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220 or CPSCI-230 or CPSCI-240; and MATH-216; and MATH-254; or instructor consent

Course Description: Introduction to the theory and implementation of Natural Language Processing (NLP). This course explores computational methods for processing, understanding, and generating human language. Students will learn to represent and process natural language, build and evaluate NLP models, and apply these models to real-world language tasks. Topics include text preprocessing and tokenization, language representations, text classification, neural language models, transformers, and large language models (LLMs).
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220 and CPSCI-230

Course Description: Introduction to the theory and implementation of artificial intelligence. This course covers both foundational and modern approaches to AI, and explores a common thread of searching intelligently for solutions. Students will learn to select an appropriate AI representation to solve a problem and empirically analyze the performance of AI systems. Topics include heuristic search, game playing, evolutionary computation, machine learning, and the ethics of artificial intelligence. Programming Intensive.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220 and CPSCI-230

Course Description: This course provides a thorough examination of the fundamental concepts underpinning all of computation. The course introduces the ideas of formal languages and computational models, and uses them to discuss computability and the existence of unsolvable problems. We develop increasingly complex models of computation, including finite automata, regular expressions, context-free grammars, and Turing machines. The course concludes with a high-level discussion of the computational complexity classes P and NP.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-230

Course Description: This course covers the fundamental concepts of data communication and computer networks. Topics include layered network architecture; reliable data transfer and transport protocols; routing and forwarding; data link layer communications and principles of shared media access. Advanced topics may include physical layer protocols, mobile networks, and software-defined radio networks. Students will apply their understanding of networking fundamentals while working on hands-on programming assignments.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-230; and must have taken or be concurrently enrolled in CPSCI-240

Course Description: Seminar in an area of computer science. Content differing from year-to-year, has included genetic programming, embedded systems, computer security, and computational geometry.
Prerequisite Narrative: A 300-level course in computer science and permission of instructor.

Course Description: Practicum in which teams of students provide computer expertise and support for faculty research projects. Topics include software engineering analysis, design, coding, testing, maintenance, and documentation.
Prerequisite Narrative: CPSCI-220, CPSCI-230, and CPSCI-240

Course Description: Reading in a field of computer science. The class will read several papers assigned weekly from research conference proceedings and journals. Classes will consist of discussions of the day's paper(s). Students will develop a comprehensive annotated bibliography and lead the daily discussions. Does not count toward the concentration or minor.
Prerequisite Narrative: Consent of instructor.
Notes: May be repeated for credit with permission of the department.

Course Description: A semester-length research project. Open to qualified senior concentrators.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three 300-level courses numbered 310 and above, 410 and consent of the department.

Course Description: Introduction to fundamental techniques of fiction and poetry. Regular writing and reading assignments as well as critiques in class.
Introduction to the techniques of realistic and non-realistic playwriting through a variety of exercises and improvisations, culminating in the writing and staging of a one-act play.
Prerequisite Narrative: Theatre 100 or Creative Writing 215.
Notes: While no prior acting experience is required, students participate in staged readings of works.

Course Description: This hands-on practicum in the Dunham Letterpress Studio will teach students the basics of letterpress printing using metal and wood type. The course will focus on setting type, operating presses, layout and design, and gaining knowledge of letterpress printing and book arts through experimentation and practice. Students will develop and produce their own projects, as well as commissioned works for visiting writers and artists. Students with prior experience will practice advanced skills. Group projects will be allowed, subject to instructor approval. There will be selected readings on book history and print culture.
For students whose work and purpose have developed sufficiently to warrant continuing work in poetry. Regular writing and reading assignments as well as critiques in class.
Prerequisite Narrative: LIT-204 and CRWR-215

Course Description: For students whose work and purpose have developed sufficiently to warrant continuing work in fiction. Regular writing and reading assignments as well as critiques in class.
Prerequisite Narrative: 215 and a 200-level course in literature.

Course Description: A creative non-fiction workshop in which students will read and discuss essays in some of the following sub-genres: memoir, travel/nature writing, food-writing, and literary journalism by a wide range of authors. Readings will provide models for student work as well as contexts in which to examine the work students generate. Part of our task will be to answer the question: What is creative non-fiction? Through a close examination of the texts we read in class, and the process of both writing and critiquing student essays, we will attempt to clarify the sometimes vague definitions of the genre.
Prerequisite Narrative: one 100-level course in literature. Recommended: CRWR 215

Course Description: This course focuses on three components: The reading of contemporary Latin American literature, analysis and identification of narrative techniques; the student’s own production of literary texts based on learned techniques; and revision and comments on peers’ writing. Students will have weekly written assignments and also will read their peers’ short stories, poetry, nonfiction, translation of literary texts, etc. The final project is a compilation of creative works and previous drafts.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.

Course Description: For students whose work and purpose have developed sufficiently to warrant advanced work in fiction or poetry. Students will construct individual projects leading to a final collection of writings in the form of a novella, a series of stories, or a series of poems. Regular writing and reading assignments, as well as critiques in class. Prerequisite, 304 and 305. Open only to senior concentrators and, if there is room, senior minors. Maximum enrollment, 8.
Notes: Open only to senior concentrators and, if there is room, senior minors.

Course Description: Independent study under the supervision of creative writing faculty, for honors candidates who qualify for and wish to pursue honors in creative writing. Students completing 498 are expected to continue their creative writing honor's project in the spring term by enrolling in 501.
Prerequisite Narrative: CRWR-215, CRWR-304, CRWR-305, and permission of Department
Notes: Students will be assigned to CW faculty for the project.

Course Description: Independent study for honors candidates in Creative Writing.
Prerequisite Narrative: CRWR-498 and approval of the department.

Course Description: An introduction to dance through both practice and theory, exploring dance as a physical, artistic, historical, and cultural form. Students will engage in movement experiences, view and discuss performances, and learn to analyze and interpret dance across multiple genres and traditions. Particular attention is given to situating dance within its historical contexts and tracing how social, political, and cultural forces shape movement practices over time. The course builds foundational skills in movement awareness, critical thinking, and cultural understanding of dance. Open to all students; no previous dance experience required.

Studio-based course that introduces students to concepts and techniques of contemporary dance. Emphasizes movement articulation, kinesthetic awareness, and originality. Alongside developing movement fluency, students will learn to analyze and situate contemporary dance within historical and cultural contexts. The course explores how technique reflects cultural values and considers the frameworks through which we understand dancing bodies.

Beginner-level study of classical ballet with a focus on ballet's basic vocabulary in both barre and center floor exercises, studio-stage directions and designations for the classical positions of the body in space. Work on such stylistic aspects of ballet as musicality, dynamics and use of the head. Readings in kinesiology pertaining to muscular alignment analysis.
The study of dance through performance of a role in a main stage dance concert.
Prerequisite Narrative: Invitation of the department
Notes: One-quarter credit per semester. May be repeated for credit.

Course Description: An introductory technique course exploring jazz dance as a form grounded in Black American cultural and performance traditions. Students develop foundational skills in rhythm, coordination, and jazz vocabulary while situating studio practice within the historical evolution of jazz dance. Attention is given to stylistic nuance, musicality, and expressive range within jazz movement. Open to all students; no previous dance experience required.

An introduction to the development and use of sound in its relationship to performance. Topics include creation of original sound/movement structures, using vocal/body sounds as well as found objects; introduction to sound recording and the digital-audio workstation;  aural analyses of music from a variety of genres to understand certain structures and aesthetics; analyses of group pieces developed in class workshops; creation of different types of non-traditional sound/movement scores;creation of audio recordings to be used in conjuncti0n with performances.  Individual and group projects.
Notes: No previous musical, dance, or theatre experience required.

Course Description: Study of the theatrical, social and ritual aspects of dance through cross-cultural comparisons among dance forms. Exploration and analysis of such historical issues as the evolution of dances, the struggle to preserve traditional dances and dance fusions in a global society. Lectures, discussions and films.

This course explores the moving body through multiple perspectives, examining how movement is shaped by personal experience, culture, and society. Drawing on philosophical and dance studies approaches, students consider movement as physical action while also attending to its expressive and cultural significance. Through experiential movement work, readings, written reflections, discussions, and presentations, students develop skills in observing, experiencing, and analyzing movement. Alongside this analytical work, the course emphasizes developing a stronger connection to one’s own body through physical exercises that support embodied awareness and healthy movement practices.

An investigation of the musculoskeletal system and use of biomechanical principles to improve efficiency of motor behavior. Emphasis on joint, muscular and alignment analysis. Lectures, discussions and practical application of movement concepts.

Course Name: Making Dance I: Imagery and Improvisation
Course Description: Provides an introduction to choreographic creation through imagery, improvisation, and embodied exploration. The course emphasizes developing personal movement vocabularies and creative strategies for making dance, with attention to phrasing and structure. Students will experiment with tools including music, costume, props, and basic production elements to create and refine original movement. No prior dance or choreography experience required.
Notes: Not open to students who took DANCE-305

Course Description: Contact Improvisation is a duet movement form in which practitioners communicate through touch, momentum, and weight. This studio-based class introduces basic contact improvisation (CI) techniques, including embodied listening and responding, leading and following, spontaneous decision making, and co-creation. We will also consider the broader implications inherent in CI: consent, trust, boundaries, non-hierarchical leadership, and accepting and respecting differences. Course readings and viewings contextualize the practice of CI historically, culturally, and socially, with special attention to gender, race, and disabilities/mixed abilities. Contact Improvisation is practiced by people of all ages, genders, abilities, and skill levels.

An investigation into the relationship between martial arts and dance emphasizing the abstraction of movements of self-defense into dance. The study of many cultures that utilize body awareness and movement efficiency in their performance and fighting forms.  A major component is the implementation of impact weapons such as olisi (Philippines/Malaysia) and the jo (Japan).
Prerequisite Narrative: Any dance, athletic, or martial art experience

Course Description: The study of contemporary dance incorporating technique and theory.  Emphasis on alignment and efficiency of movement focusing on increasing strength and flexibility.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-112, DANCE-113, or DANCE-114 or permission of instructor

Course Description: Continuation of the study of ballet. Technique classes are combined with studies in kinesiology, dance theory and dance criticism.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-114 or consent of instructor.

Course Description: Study of the history of ballet from the Imperial Ballet of the Tsars to the present.  Study of Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, New York City Ballet, American Ballet Theatre, the Royal Ballet of England and the Kirov and Bolshoi of Russia.  Examination of aesthetic principles and their influence on the development of modern ballet.  Study of dancers, choreographers, composers and visual artists associated with the ballet world.

Builds on foundational jazz technique through more complex movement phrases, increased technical demands, and greater stylistic range. The course continues to engage jazz dance as a form rooted in Black American cultural and performance traditions, emphasizing musicality, rhythmic clarity, and dynamic nuance. Students deepen their understanding of jazz vocabulary while further situating studio practice within the historical evolution of jazz dance.
Prerequisite Narrative: Previous dance technique course or consent of instructor

Course Description: Study of the history North American Black vernacular dance forms with a predominant emphasis on jazz dance history as their progenitor. Exploration, investigation, and analysis of social, cultural, and aesthetic concepts and principles prevalent in Black vernacular forms and histories. Study of important and innovative jazz dancers, choreographers, and legacies within the jazz dance continuum. Material engagement modalities will include readings, lectures, discussions, films/video clips, and creative assignments.

An intermediate choreographic course centered on the craft of composition: space, time, structure, texture, and dynamics. Through sustained studio practice, students will generate, organize, and refine movement material, exploring how compositional choices shape the experience of a dance. The course includes close study of professional choreography to inform students’ creative processes. It culminates in each student presenting a fully realized original dance work.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-305 or consent of instructor

Course Description: A continuation of DANCE 208, emphasizing martial arts from Africa, Asia, Southeast Asia, and South America. Students will study cultural background, history, philosophy and terminology along with practical application of movement theories.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-208 or consent of instructor

Course Description: The study of contemporary dance incorporating technique and theory.  Emphasis on performance techniques and ability to comprehend the conceptual framework of movement.  Supplemental training in Pilates, jazz, and yoga. Guest artists invited each year to teach master classes.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-213 or consent of instructor.
Notes: Required for students to perform in a faculty or guest artist's work for the Family Weekend Concert. May be repeated for credit.

Course Description: The study of classical ballet emphasizing style and performance quality in addition to technical mastery of the ballet vocabulary.  Meets five times weekly. While out-of-class assignments are minimal, daily attendance, effort and consistent improvement in the technical and stylistic aspects of this art form are of critical importance.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-215 or consent of instructor.

Course Name: Advanced Media: Electronic and Choreographic Assemblages
Course Description: Construction of hybrid artworks that commingle digital, analog and choreographic media to explore ideas of transmission, networks, collaboration, process, and interdependence. Study of assemblage across 20th & 21st century art practices. Emphasis on philosophy, embodied cognition, affect theory, and critical media theory in considering how assemblage might offer us alternative modes of relating to and augmenting the technologies that shape our lives. Projects will include circuit bending, projection mapping, non-binary machines, sculpture, participatory art practice, artificial intelligence, and experimental performance.
Prerequisite Narrative: DARTS-231 / MUSIC-231 / THETR-231 or ART-240 / DARTS-240 / MUSIC-240 / THETR-240
Prerequisites: DARTS-231, , MUSIC-231, , THETR-231, , ART-240, , DARTS-240, , MUSIC-240, , THETR-240,

Course Name: Advanced Martial Arts and Dance II
Course Description: A further continuation and development of skills and knowledge that were learned in 208/308, with more emphasis on individual exploration, and creative work. Martial cultures/performance forms originating in China, Brazil, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Japan will be the main focus for source material. Historical, cultural, and philosophical readings will add to further understanding of these approaches.
Prerequisite Narrative: DANCE-208, DANCE-308, or consent of the instructor

Course Description: A research paper or a field study in movement behavior and its analysis/notation.

A performance of dance works, the choreography of dance works or both. Substantial written component comprising research into the historical, theoretical and socio-cultural contexts of the chosen work. Following submission of the monograph and completion of production, each student will participate in the evaluation of her/his project with an evaluating committee.

Course Name: Ways of Seeing: Vision, Technology, Media
Course Description: An introduction to the study of media with a focus on visual media and experience. Students will learn about key moments in media history, from the invention of print to the rise of broadcasting/mass media and the entrenchment of digital/social media. Students will engage with foundational concepts in media and visual studies, and develop tools to critically analyze, discuss, and write about the images that come to us through physical and virtual networks. Topics include: photojournalism, infographics, screen cultures, public relations and advertising, social media, AI, and the effects of digital media on the environment and mental health.

Course Name: Introduction to Media: Integrated Media and Emerging Practices
Course Description: This course will serve as an introduction to digital technology in contemporary art making as it relates to interactivity, collaboration, and emerging practices.  Emphasis will be placed on hands on experimentation and exploration across disciplines. We will cover installation art, web art, digital and time-based art, and immersive environments. Students will gain an overview of emerging digital practices, collaborative production strategies and correlations to social, aesthetic and theoretical issues. Other topics may include virtuality, performance, cyborgs, and network culture.

Course Name: From Cybernetics to AI: Art, Media, and the Global Histories of Data Processing
Course Description: Artificial intelligence and data processing systems shape everyday life, but how did they come about? How did mathematicians, engineers, artists, and designers imagine computer-controlled worlds before they were even possible? And how can their ideas help us raise questions about digital rights, data security, and data justice today? We will explore the media history of data processing and its global transformations through computer art, concrete poetry, experimental media and science fiction films from Germany, Latin America, and the Soviet Union from the 1960s to the present. Our theoretical discussions will be grounded in readings on cybernetics, a theory of communication and control that shaped early computing, but also forged interdisciplinary connections with biology, sociology, literature and art through terms such as “feedback” and “self-regulation.” This course is specifically aimed at students who want to discover how the sciences and the humanities interact to gain new, creative impulses for their own thinking.
Introduction to fundamentals of craft and study of experimental video. Emphasis on developing ideas and conveying meaning through video art, working outside commercial traditions.

The invention of photography in the 1820s was one of the most important revolutions of modernity, and it changed just about everything, including how we define art, how process the news, how we relate to people and places, and how we remember the past. This interdisciplinary, active learning course equips students with the ability to analyze photographs as images and as material objects, and to identify the technologies and social practices that have made photography ubiquitous. Topics span the 19th-21st centuries and include portraiture; travel photography; scientific imaging; photojournalism and the paparazzi; crime and surveillance; advertising and fashion; the art market for photographs; the shift from analog to digital; and machine vision and AI.

An introduction to the history, tools and language of basic animation styles. This course will trace the history of experiments in animated imagery from 19th Century photography through 20th Century film into 21st Century digital works. The class will cover basic techniques in Photoshop, Adobe Premier, and illustration and animation software interfaces.

Course Name: Intermediate Media: New Frontiers in Storytelling
Course Description: This class will survey and create emergent and non -linear forms of storytelling using digital and hybrid tools. We will examine notions of narrative authority and hybridity in a digital age and think through different ways we might use technology to distill, break apart or reify modes of communication and visual metaphor. Discussion will push boundaries of traditional storytelling and consider connectivity, liveness and embodied presence. This course will draw on multiple forms of expression including but not limited to digital media, performance, sound, XR, web, and network environments.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any intro-level Digital Arts studio course, including cross-listed.
Prerequisites: ART-113, , DARTS-113, , MUSIC-113, , ART 116, , DARTS-212, , ART-213, , DARTS-213, , ART-221, , DARTS-221, , MUSIC-270,

Course Name: Intermediate Media: Performance, Ritual and Technology
Course Description: This class will cover performance strategies in relationship to digital technology, ritual and the social. We will create collaborative and hybrid work at the intersection of performance, digital media and social practice and map out modes of ritual engagement within these intersections.  We will explore "liveness" as a digital and/or embodied presence and survey contemporary hybrid performance work.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any intro-level Digital Arts course, including cross-listed.
Prerequisites: DARTS-113, , DARTS-212, , DARTS-213, , DARTS-221, , DARTS-231, , ART 116, , MUSIC-270,

Course Description: This seminar examines key moments in the history of documentary photography. We will focus on the people and institutions that have used photography to shed light on social injustices and promote systematic change from the 19th century to the present day. And, we will trace how the practice of documentary has been defined, critiqued, and redefined in that time. Students will read foundational and new scholarship on documentary photography; examine physical media, including magazines and photo books, where documentary photographs appeared; and conduct research utilizing digital archives of documentary photographs.

Course Name: Advanced Media: Robot Musicals and AI Techno Opera
Course Description: This class is an advanced workshop exploring possible uses of Artificial Intelligence in devised musical theater creation. Students will participate in community sourced and collaborative performance building, explore human/ technological interfaces, and discuss Artificial Intelligence, scores, algorithms and their potential to support improvisation, and theater creation. In addition, this workshop will establish the compositional framework for a work-in-progress AI techno opera; enrolled students are invited into this continuing process as active collaborators with the core team of artists. The class welcomes performers, computer programmers, musicians, technologists, and singers--anyone with an interest in cross-disciplinary collaboration.
Prerequisite Narrative: DARTS-231 / MUSIC-231 / THETR-231 or ART-240 / DARTS-240 / MUSIC-240 / THETR-240
Prerequisites: DARTS-231, , MUSIC-231, , THETR-231, , ART-240, , DARTS-240, , MUSIC-240, , THETR-240,

Course Name: Magazines: Digital Approaches to Print Media
Course Description: How can digital tools help us understand print visual culture? This research lab-style seminar integrates humanistic inquiry with a collaborative research and project design process integral to STEM fields. Students will read cutting edge work on illustrated magazines including Life, Vogue, and National Geographic and explore digital humanities projects that offer new ways to explore histories of print media. Students will learn about the possibilities and limits of digital tools such as mapping, network visualizations, and text mining, and design their own projects utilizing digitized collections of illustrated magazines.
Advanced investigation and study of experimental video production. Exploration of personal vision combined with emphasis on social and cultural contexts for video.
Prerequisite Narrative: ART-213
Notes: May repeat for credit at increasingly advanced levels with permission of the professor.

Course Name: Advanced Media: Electronic and Choreographic Assemblages
Course Description: Construction of hybrid artworks that commingle digital, analog and choreographic media to explore ideas of transmission, networks, collaboration, process, and interdependence. Study of assemblage across 20th & 21st century art practices. Emphasis on philosophy, embodied cognition, affect theory, and critical media theory in considering how assemblage might offer us alternative modes of relating to and augmenting the technologies that shape our lives. Projects will include circuit bending, projection mapping, non-binary machines, sculpture, participatory art practice, artificial intelligence, and experimental performance.
Prerequisite Narrative: DARTS-231 / MUSIC-231 / THETR-231 or ART-240 / DARTS-240 / MUSIC-240 / THETR-240
Prerequisites: DARTS-231, , MUSIC-231, , THETR-231, , ART-240, , DARTS-240, , MUSIC-240, , THETR-240,

Course Name: Advanced Media: TV Club: Media Collectives, Live Streaming, Performance and Video
Course Description: This advanced Digital Media class will take place between the Digital Arts Lab, and the Photo/Video studio. The focus will be on live mediated performance broadcasts, and will address histories of public access television, broadcast media, media collectives, social and activist video art, and social implications of a recent return back to livestreaming via the internet. Additional topics covered will include digital and analog tools for live video processing, interactivity and studio audiences, serial TV and internet show formats, green screen techniques, and narrative strategies that utilize the integration of bodies, music, props and media in real time. The course will include weekly internet live streams of student work to the Hamilton community and beyond.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any DARTS 100- or 200-level course (including cross-listed departments), or THETR-100, or THETR-105

Course Description: Emphasis on collaborative work among Digital Arts and video students in the creation of visual/sound works. Projects will include fixed media works, installations, and performance art pieces.
Prerequisite Narrative: DARTS-113 / ART-113 / MUSIC-113,  ART-213 / DARTS-213, ART-221 / DARTS-221, DARTS-231 / MUSIC-231 / THETR-231, or DARTS-240
Prerequisites: DARTS-113, , ART-113, , MUSIC-113, , ART-213, , DARTS-213, , ART-221, , DARTS-221, , DARTS-231, , MUSIC-231, , THETR-231, , DARTS-240,

Course Description: This course focuses on foundational concepts in Data Science. Students are introduced to key mathematical, computational, and statistical principles and how they are applied in modern data science. Topics include data wrangling, the data management lifecycle, core concepts in statistical computing, basic vector and matrix algebra, and an introduction to optimization. Students will apply these concepts to machine learning and statistical analysis through a variety of projects. Additional topics will be covered depending on student interest and instructor expertise.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-116 and MATH-254
Instructor: Bowman, Kropp, Kuruwita, Tripp (and eventually others on the program committee/who contribute to the program regularly)

Course Description: The price system as a mechanism for determining which goods will be produced and which inputs employed; decision-making by firms and individuals; market structure; Gross domestic product; its measurement and the determination of production and employment levels; the role of the government in the economy.

An introduction to how economists develop and test theory, with a special emphasis on theory explaining the causes and consequences of inequality. The basic concepts of probability and statistics are taught in addition to theories of the labor market, inflation/unemployment tradeoffs, impact of fiscal and monetary policy, externalities, public goods, and international trade.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-100
Notes: Not open to seniors or students who have taken MATH 152, MATH 254, or GOVT 230.

Course Description: This course covers topics related to household decision-making and how these decisions impact the environment. Throughout the course, students will learn about different models of household behavior and how they predict investment in energy-efficient technologies. Students will then examine environmental policies, how they interact with household incentives and budget constraints, and the impact that these policies have on social welfare.
Notes: Does not count toward the concentration or minor.

Course Description: Investigates policies to alleviate poverty, with a focus on the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC).  Topics include:  poverty, income inequality and inequality of opportunity; tax policy; and incentives created by policies aimed at alleviating poverty.  The class has a significant service learning component in which students complete IRS training at the Basic level and assist low-income families in Utica in filling out Federal tax forms to claim the EITC.
Prerequisite Narrative: None
Notes: The course meets one hour per week through April 15, with a minimum in-class time of 10 hours. Requires significant self-paced training prior to start of classes. Course can only be taken on a Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory basis. Does not count toward the concentration or minor. Course taught concurrently with ECON 236. May be retaken once for credit with instructor consent.

Course Description: Investigates policies to alleviate poverty, with a focus on the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC). Topics include: poverty, income inequality and inequality of opportunity; tax policy; and incentives created by policies aimed at alleviating poverty. The class has a significant service learning component in which students complete IRS (Advanced) training and assist low-income families in Utica in filling out Federal tax forms to claim the EITC.
Prerequisite Narrative: Completion of 0.5 credits of ECON 235
Notes: The course meets one hour per week through April 15, with a minimum in-class time of 10 hours. Requires significant self-paced training prior to start of classes. Course can only be taken on a Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory basis. Does not count toward the concentration or minor. Course taught concurrently with ECON-235. May be retaken once for credit with instructor consent.

Course Description: An introduction to econometric methods that are frequently used in applied economic research.  Emphasis on interpreting and critically evaluating empirical results and on establishing the statistical foundations of widely used econometric methods.  Topics include the classical linear regression model, functional form, dummy explanatory variables, binary choice models, panel data models, instrumental variables and time series models.  Three hours of class and 75 minutes of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor
Notes: Not open to seniors or students who have taken ECON 400.

Course Description: The theory of consumer behavior. Theories of the firm and market structures, and of resource allocation, pricing and income distribution. General equilibrium and economic efficiency.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 and MATH-113 or the equivalent.

Course Description: Theories of business cycles and economic growth. Theories of monetary policy, budget and trade balances, aggregate consumption and investment activity, unemployment, inflation, technological change and productivity growth.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: A study of the economics behind money, financial markets and the macroeconomy and how they are connected. How do financial markets work and how is the interest rate determined? Examination of the role of banks and other financial institutions in the economy. Analyzing the role of the Federal Reserve in the financial system, conduct of monetary policy and monetary theory.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: Analysis of the role of government in the economy from both the expenditure side and the income (tax) side. Topics include public goods, externalities, the U.S. "safety net," social security, government involvement in health care, public choice, budget deficits,the U.S. tax system, and the effects of taxation and government programs on behavior.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166
Notes: Not open to students who have taken ECON-440.

Course Description: Examines health and healthcare policies with an economic perspective. Topics covered include 1) delivery of healthcare across the world, 2) government involvement and, 3) current proposed policies or policy reforms. This course emphasizes the development of professional presentation and discussion skills, teaching students to communicate to a wide range of audience while also teaching students to discuss thoughtfully and respectfully topics where opposing views often arise.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: Examines differences in economic outcomes by race, gender, sexual orientation, religion, or other personal characteristic. Topics include 1) identification of discrimination in different markets including (but not limited to) the labor, education, and credit/housing market, and 2) evaluation of the effectiveness of policies aimed at reducing discrimination. This course places a special emphasis on developing professional presentation and discussion skills, teaching students to discuss controversial topics in a thoughtful and respectful manner.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Name: The Economics of Technology and Innovation
Course Description: An examination of the nature and implications of innovation and technological change. We will investigate the history and economic theory of innovation and technological progress, related policy debates, and future prospects. Particular attention to the implications of recent developments in information technology and robotics for labor markets and the distribution of economic wellbeing.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Description: Theoretical and empirical analysis of the pattern of international trade and international trade policies. Emphasis on theoretical models used by economists. Topics include the determinants of the pattern of international trade, immigration, foreign direct investment, the gains from trade, tariffs, quotas, voluntary export restraints, dumping, subsidies, trade-related intellectual property rights, international labor standards, trade and environmental issues, the WTO, customs unions, free trade agreements and  trade adjustment assistance.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor
Notes: Not open to students who are or have taken ECON-433.

Course Description: This course explores fundamental questions in international economics, including the determinants of the current account and the real exchange rate, the implications of fixed and flexible exchange rate regimes, and the interactions between monetary and fiscal policy. In line with current economic research, the course uses a microfounded framework to analyze real-world international macroeconomic issues.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: Rather than assume that people, firms, or leaders are always purely rational, behavioral economics relaxes this assumption and analyzes situations where rationality does not always hold.   The field integrates research across disciplines, drawing from neuroscience, behavioral and developmental psychology, and economics.  As such it allows economists to study why people choose outcomes that seem to violate traditionally held views of rationality and why markets actually behave as they do. It allows economists to better understand how individuals, groups, and firms respond to policies.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Description: Introduction to the study of international development. Topics include economic growth, poverty, inequality, public health challenges, demography, education, child labor, environmental decay and climate change, urbanization and global cities, agriculture and food security, conflict, and corruption.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Description: Integrates space into traditional economics models and focuses on the role that location plays in the decision-making of firms and individuals. Topics include why cities form, why people choose to live in cities, and what policies can alter the shape, size, and economic success of cities. Covers a range of challenges that arise when people live in cities such as the provision of public goods, poverty and inequality, transportation and congestion, crime, housing discrimination, and education. Analyzes ways in which we can address these challenges through evidence-based urban policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: A study of the goals, strategies and tactics of monetary policy. The interaction of the central bank with financial markets, the tools and the transmission mechanism of monetary policy, and structure of the Federal Reserve System and the international financial system. Emphasis on policy application.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Name: Economics of Poverty and Income Distribution
Course Description: A study of domestic poverty and of government programs designed to address poverty. Topics include the definition and measurement of poverty, the factors associated with becoming poor and the design, purpose, financing and individual incentive effects of various state and federal public assistance programs, as well as their effectiveness in reducing the incidence or duration of poverty.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Description: An analysis of the economics of health and medical care, with particular emphasis on the provision of health care in the United States. Topics include the structure of public and private health insurance programs, financing the rising costs of medical care and the impact of health status on labor supply and retirement decisions. Relates these issues to current public policy debates surrounding the health care profession.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Description: An analysis of economic and financial crises including the Panic of 1907, the Great Depression, the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, and the Global Financial Crisis.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166
Notes: For each crisis, we will explore the background leading up to the crisis, how the crisis unfolded, how policymakers responded, and the long lasting impact of the crisis.

Course Description: An examination and explanation of the development of the American economy, focusing on the period from 1840 through World War II. Topics include the economics of slavery and share cropping, the rise of big business, railroads and economic growth, the development of banks and the causes of the Great Depression.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: A survey of topics in economic history that help us understand a classic and important question “what determines the wealth of nations”? Topics and papers were chosen to give a broad perspective on growth and development in economic history, such as the divergence in income per capita and improvements in health and literacy. It will thus be largely thematic instead of chronological and not limited to one area. We will cover research primarily by economic historians on topics such as the causes of the British Industrial Revolution, colonialism, slavery in the United States, infrastructure and public health, and human capital formation.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: A survey of economic theory and methodology from the early Greeks to the present. Discussion of the ideas of major economic writers such as Smith, Marx, Marshall and Keynes, with attention paid to historical context as well as relevance to current economic debates.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Name: Political Economy of Environmental and Energy Policy
Course Description: Markets, individual preferences, and political structures all play a key role in shaping environmental and energy policy. In this course, we will adopt a multi-level political economy approach that draws on behavioral economics to understand individual environmental preferences and works upward through electoral politics and institutional structures. Students will work with economic theory to understand predicted policy effects, and polling and congressional voting data to understand the factors that shape environmental policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-100 and ECON-166

Course Description: An examination of issues in environmental policy from the perspective of economic theory. Topics include the measurement of benefits and costs of curtailing pollution and preserving ecosystems, the design of public policies to improve environmental quality, and the examination of past and current environmental programs in the United States and their success. Also considers sustainable growth and issues of environmental equity.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166 or consent of instructor

Course Description: This course is an introduction to the basic models and empirical strategies used to study labor economics and related public policy and institutions. Topics include labor supply and demand, taxes and transfers, unemployment, education and job training, discrimination and associated affirmative action and diversity, equity, and inclusion policies, wage inequality, minimum wage laws, social mobility, labor unions, household decision making, flexible work arrangements, and automation.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-166

Course Description: An advanced treatment of selected topics of current interest in macroeconomics. Theoretical and empirical approaches to understanding recent recessions and trends in economic growth, technological change, unemployment, inflation, financial conditions, income inequality, and macroeconomic policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: This course focuses on monetary and fiscal policy interactions. It covers economic theory and empirical facts about monetary and fiscal regimes, inflation, government deficits and debt in the United States, the European Union and emerging economies.  Students will learn to examine the existing literature critically. There will be frequent discussions of journal articles and their policy implications. The focus will be on learning how to use economic theory and statistical methods to formulate and test hypotheses.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: A study of issues in the economics of higher education.  Topics will include the financing of higher education, determinants of tuition costs, trends in admissions policies, determinants of academic success at college, and the economic returns to higher education.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: This course covers environmental and natural resource economics topics such as common-pool resources, non-market valuation, carbon prices, environmental justice, and decarbonizing electricity generation. Students will learn to examine the existing literature critically. There will be frequent discussions of journal articles and their policy implications. The focus will be on learning how to use economic theory and statistical methods to formulate and test hypotheses.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: Theoretical and empirical study of the determinants of happiness, life satisfaction, mental health, and other subjective measures of well-being. Topics include the measurement and reliability of well-being measures, the relationship between well-being and economic variables such as income and employment, and differences in well-being across various demographic groups.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: A study of issues in the economics of education, using microeconomic theory and empirical methods to analyze K-12 education policy. Topics include: the determinants of school quality, how to find and retain effective teachers, the effects of school accountability programs on student achievement, the role of charter schools and school choice in the provision of high-quality public education, and the consequences of more widespread early childhood education. Students will learn to read and critique empirical research to understand its implications for policy, focusing on the experimental and quasi-experimental methods most commonly used by applied microeconomists.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: Students will learn about some of the challenges faced by people in developing countries, and about the tools used to assess the interventions designed to confront them. The course will be mostly empirical—students will critically read research papers and learned about the methods frequently used by applied microeconomists.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Name: Topics in the Economics of Gender and Sexual Orientation
Course Description: This course will use microeconomic theory, statistical methods, and recent empirical work to examine the causes and consequences of gender and sexual orientation differences in economic outcomes. We will study a variety of topics including education, labor supply, marriage, household, and family choices. This course will 1) examine the history and current state of affairs of gender and sexual orientation differences 2) evaluate policy and its impacts on outcomes.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: What would be the impact of a 1°C rise in global temperature on world GDP, and for how long? What impact would a 1% increase in interest rates have on inflation over the next year? How can a retail business predict sales for the next 3–5 years based on its current marketing strategy? Time series econometrics provides the tools to answer such questions by combining statistical methods and economic theory to analyze data over time. It helps identify patterns, forecast trends, and make informed decisions, making it essential for understanding economic dynamics and policy implications. This course introduces the econometrics of time series analysis for forecasting and estimating dynamic causal effects using Python.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: A study of individual level investment decisions and the equilibrium determination of asset prices. Mean-variance analysis motivated by the tradeoff between risk and return. An introduction to asset pricing models, including the CAPM and multi-factor models. An introduction to derivatives, including stock options, futures and swaps. Discussions of the Efficient Markets Hypothesis, arbitrage, and contributions from behavioral finance. Other topics may include: fixed income pricing, Arrow-Debreu securities and the completeness of markets, and the binomial asset pricing model.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285, or consent of instructor

Course Description: This course covers a broad range of theories and issues in international finance, including the evolution of the current global financial markets, balance of payments problems, exchange rate determination and currency markets, financial and currency crisis, international capital flows, international banking, and macroeconomic policies in an open economy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-285

Course Description: This course covers topics in international trade and international finance. We will investigate the causes and consequences of international trade, explore policies that regulate international trade and their effect on economic welfare, as well as study the international flow of financial assets across countries. Students will learn to examine the existing literature critically. There will be frequent discussions of journal articles and their policy implications. The focus will be on learning how to use economic theory and statistical methods to formulate and test hypotheses.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266,  ECON-275, and ECON-285
Notes: Not available to student who are or have taken ECON-432.

Course Description: Theoretical and empirical analysis of firm conduct with emphasis on firms in oligopolistic industries. Examination of conduct primarily, but not entirely, from a game theory perspective. Exploration of business practices such as product differentiation and advertising, research and development, and price discrimination. Consideration of relevant public policies, especially antitrust policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275 or consent of instructor

Course Name: Topics in Economic History and Political Economy
Course Description: This course covers topics related to political decision making and its implications for economic development as well as economic and policy outcomes today. We cover theoretical and empirical approaches to collective decision-making, institutions and the state, technological change, property rights, issues in democracies, issues in non-democracies. Students will learn to use theory to understand political issues and examine research articles critically.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: This course examines the economic history of the United States and its relevance for understanding contemporary policy and economic outcomes. We will study topics such as migration, transportation, education, innovation, industrial development, inequality, and the role of culture. These topics will be situated within major historical periods, including the Westward Expansion, slavery and the Civil War, Reconstruction, the Great Depression and the New Deal, World War I and the interwar years, World War II, and the postwar era. Students will critically read research papers and learn about the empirical methods used in applied microeconomics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: Is it possible to sustain infinite economic growth on a finite planet? This course uses tools from economics to answer that question. Topics will include the importance of finite inputs in production, whether the externalities of economic growth prevent sustained growth, and climate change. We will study the role that government intervention can or cannot play in promoting sustainable economic growth.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-285

Course Description: The course addresses the role of governments and government policies in the U.S. economy and on individual behavior.  You will develop an understanding of the theories of taxation and government expenditure and their impact on a wide range of real-world problems and situations.  Topics include market failures; voting behavior and its implications for resource allocation, expenditure program evaluation, the incidence and efficiency of various taxes, and redistribution of income polices such as public assistance and Social Security.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: Why are some countries so rich while others are so poor? Examines the difference in living standards both across and within countries, using both theoretical and empirical methods. Topics include the effects of income distribution, technology, population growth, international trade, government policy and culture on the level and growth of per capita income.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: A study of the goals, strategies and tactics of monetary policy. The interaction of the central bank with financial markets, the tools and the transmission mechanism of monetary policy, and structure of the Federal Reserve System and the international financial system. Emphasis on policy application. Students in the class have the opportunity to participate in the College Fed Challenge, a national competition in which teams of students make a presentation to monetary policy experts about the current state of the economy and the future course of monetary policy. (Oral Presentations.)
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-285

Course Description: A study of issues in economic development as they apply to Latin America. Topics include poverty, inequality, education and health. Students will learn about the methods used to assess different social policies.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275 or consent of instructor

Course Description: An introduction to theories of strategic behavior as they have been developed and applied in economics. Applications include strategic behavior in oligopolistic markets, auctions, bargaining, trade policy, procrastination, standards setting and the provision of public goods.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275 or consent of the instructor

Course Name: Economics of Human Resource Management Practices
Course Description: Theoretical and empirical study of human resource management including: the choice of the form of labor compensation (e.g. fixed wage, salary, piece rates and other forms of pay for performance); the effects on firm performance of employee involvement programs (e.g., self-directed teams) and of financial participation schemes (e.g., profit sharing and employee stock ownership); hiring; training; promotions; and the level and structure of executive compensation and corporate governance.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: This course introduces students to economic inquiry using experimental methodologies.  Experimental economics is a relatively new field in which decision making is examined in a controlled laboratory setting.  The data from these experiments are used to evaluate theories as well as to test and fine tune policies that could not be easily tested with naturally-occurring data.  Students will learn how to combine theories from behavioral economics and experimental methodologies to help them answer the economic questions they want to research.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275

Course Description: Topics will include: defining labor markets; labor market participation and intensity; the impact of technological change on labor demand; impacts of minimum wages; returns to all investments in education and on the job training; immigration and labor turnover; effects of gender, race and ethnicity in labor markets; economic effects of labor unions; the increase in inequality and changes in labor markets; the effects of employee participation and employee ownership on enterprise performance and outcomes for employees.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to international finance.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285
Notes: Co-Requisite ECON-432. Open to concentrators only.

Course Name: Senior Project in Economics of Human Resource Management Practices
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to the economics of human resource management practices.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to macroeconomics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285
Notes: Open to concentrators only. Co-requisite ECON-413.

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to the development economics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to long-run economic growth.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285
Notes: Co-Requisite ECON-445. Open to concentrators only.

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to industrial organization. Open to concentrators only.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, ECON-285 and consent of instructor

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to public economics. Open to concentrators only.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Name: Senior Project in Economics of Happiness
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to the economics of subjective well-being.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to environmental economics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285
Notes: Open to concentrators only. Co-requisite ECON-417.

Course Name: Senior Project in Behavioral and Experimental Economics
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to behavioral and/or experimental economics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to financial economics, macro-finance, or central bank policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, ECON-285

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to international economics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275 and ECON-285

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to macroeconomic policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275 and ECON-285

Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to labor economics.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Name: Senior Project in the Economics of Education
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to the economics of education. Open to concentrators only.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Name: Senior Project in Economics of Gender and Sexual Orientation
Course Description: This course examines the causes and consequences of gender and sexual orientation differences in economic outcomes such as education, labor supply, marriage, household, and family choices. This class satisfies the senior project requirement through an empirical study closely related to a topic covered in the Topics in Economics of Gender and Sexual Orientation.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON 266 and ECON 275

Course Name: Senior Project in Economic History and Political Economy
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to economic history and political economy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON 266 and ECON 275

Course Name: Senior Project in American Economic History
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to American economic history.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266 and ECON-275

Course Name: Senior Project in Sustainable Economic Growth
Course Description: A senior project for concentrators in the department. Students will work on projects related to sustainability, environmental policy, and economic growth.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285

Course Description: Each student works intensively on a topic chosen in consultation with the instructor. Weekly meetings held to hear progress reports and to discuss research techniques pertinent to student topics. Candidates for honors must complete this course.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-266, ECON-275, ECON-285, and permission of the department

Course Description: What is education? What is school? How do we critically understand education and schools? What are the possibilities and limitations of education for change and justice? Emphasis on, but not limited to, American education. Includes lecture, discussion, multi-media projects, and small-group interaction.

What is education?  How is education manifested in individuals, schools, and society?  We’ll start the term by examining the nature of knowledge.  Then, we’ll turn to how people learn, before proceeding to think about how we can teach others.  Finally, we’ll look at schools, how they are and how they could be.  We’ll focus on philosophical questions at the roots of education and learning.  Readings will be both historical and contemporary and will include a diverse range of views.

Course Name: Methods of Tutoring English to Speakers of Other Languages
Course Description: Familiarizes students with ESOL (English for Speakers of Other Languages) methods and materials. Emphasis on adapting them for tutorial use in various settings including distanced learning. Close examination of refugee communities with primary focus on Utica. Study of cultural, educational, and social effects of refugees.  Course may be repeated for credit.
Notes: Course provides students with the Hamilton College ESOL Tutor Certificate of Completion. One hourly session per week and 20 field study and/or service learning hours required. One-quarter course credit. Evaluated Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory.

Course Name: Methods of Tutoring English to Speakers of Other Languages II
Course Description: Familiarizes students with ESOL (English for Speakers of Other Languages) methods and materials. Emphasis on adapting them for tutorial use in various settings. Close examination of refugee communities with primary focus on Utica. Study of cultural, educational, and social effects of refugees.  Course may be repeated for credit.
Notes: 20 field study and/or service learning hours required. One-quarter course credit. Evaluated Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory.

Course Description: This course provides an understanding of the importance of ethnography to the consideration of issues introduced in EDUC-102. What is ethnography as a methodology for exploring education? Students will practice methods such as participant observation, interviews, and oral history through in-class exercises, as well as conduct an ethnographic project of their own.
Prerequisite Narrative: EDUC-102 or consent of instructor

Course Description: Shaped by social, political, and economic forces, urban schools reflect diverse societal issues and inequalities.  In this course, students will first examine the historical foundation in which issues and inequalities in urban schools are rooted by exploring such topics as urban development and distribution of economic opportunity, migration, immigration, segregation, housing and rezoning.  Next, students will explore how inequalities impact urban schools and then how experiences in urban schools reproduce inequalities of access and opportunity to education.
Prerequisite Narrative: Educ 200, an introductory social science course, or permission of instructor

Course Name: Pedagogy, Power and the Politics of Knowledge
Course Description: Whose knowledge matters? How do students experience claims to knowledge? How does critical pedagogy disrupt traditional hierarchies in educational institutions and foster the inclusion and engagement of multiple voices, experiences and diverse knowledge? This course explores of the theories and praxis of critical pedagogy. Oppression, privilege, power and critical points of transformation will be examined in context of curriculum, instruction, and students' classroom experiences across education contexts (K-12 and higher education).
Prerequisite Narrative: introductory course in Education Studies or consent of instructor.

Course Description: Just what is a university, understood anthropologically? How do we understand its many subcultures, its organizational forms, its economies and its ideological functions? In this course, we will critically examine these questions, and discuss how "the university" is shaped by forces of globalization, migration, neoliberalism, and discourses of diversity. We will read ethnographies about "the university", analyzing how "the university," as a cultured institution, produces and reproduces various forms of inequality as well as generates new forms of subjectivity.
Prerequisite Narrative: ANTHR-113 or EDUC-102
Notes: May be taught as an FYC at the discretion of the department. No prerequisites when taught as an FYC.

Course Description: The research and scholarship of curricular decision-making is studied to better understand the form and substance of the American public school.  Federal and state regulations, standards, and testing processes will be considered when looking at innovative and sometimes controversial curricular plans and models. Case studies, curriculum development activities, and oral reports are used.
Prerequisite Narrative: 200 or permission of instructor.

Course Description: Investigates the social experiences and mediatized representations of Muslim youth through ethnography and multimodal artifacts. Emphasizes deconstructing the semiotics of the "Muslim" figure in public discourse to understand, and critique, how this construction leads to various forms of anti-Muslim racism, but also attending to the forms of response and resistance from Muslim youth.
Prerequisite Narrative: Anth 113.

Course Description: This course provides a sociological lens for analyzing education and educational inequality in the United States. Over the course of the semester, we will use various theories to explore education as a social institution, going beyond our own individual experiences and personal ideologies. In addition to covering the foundational ideas in the sociology of education, we will spend considerable time exploring the myriad ways that education impacts, and is impacted by, broader patterns of inequality. We will also use empirical studies to examine external factors that affect student experiences and shape learning outcomes; factors such as the role of families, neighborhoods, and schools, themselves. Salient topics include racial segregation, economic stratification within and between schools, technology, tracking, teacher pedagogy, immigration, English Language Learners, punishment, higher education, and the future of education in a demographically and culturally diversifying society.
Prerequisite Narrative: SOC-101, SOC-110, or SOC-126

Course Name: Educating Students with Disabilities/Policy and Practice
Course Description: This course primarily focuses on the needs of students with educational disabilities, health care needs and students from diverse cultural, socioeconomic, and linguistic backgrounds.  Aspects of the course include identifying students’ strengths and needs, differentiating and/or individualizing instruction, collaborating with educators and service professionals, and delivering instruction that is universally designed to maximize access for all learners.

Course Name: POV: You're Not the Main Character
Course Description: What does it mean to listen to someone you disagree with? Why do some conversations bring people together while others deepen division? And can we learn to disagree without dehumanizing one another? In a time of polarization, cultural conflict, and competing ideas about belonging, this course explores dialogue as a practice for navigating difference and strengthening democratic life. Drawing on intergroup dialogue and critical theories of identity, power, and socialization, students examine how our experiences shape what we believe and how we understand others. Through storytelling, dialogue, reflection, and engagement with contested issues, students will learn to listen deeply, ask better questions, navigate discomfort and conflict, and connect interpersonal experiences to larger social systems. Ultimately, the course asks: If we understand one another differently, what becomes possible?

A survey of fundamental concepts in education through historical and contemporary texts.  We start by thinking about the goals of education, including knowledge, virtue, and skills.  Next, we consider human capacities for learning before turning to the nature of learning and various approaches to teaching.  Finally, we look at the relation between schools and society and consider how to design more effective institutions for learning.  Knowledge and Education is a team-based learning class.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy or Education Studies
Notes: Not open to students who have completed PHIL-124: Philosophy of Education.

Course Name: Online Teaching and Learning: Theories, Models, and Design
Course Description: No longer an alternate methodology or supplemental approach for K-16 education, the dominant emergence of online learning now requires an accelerated set of decisions around equity, inclusion, the role of teacher, learner, and technology, academic rigor and the future of the American public education system. Online learning theories and models will be examined and experienced through interviews with practitioners, readings, and application of virtual instructional design, development and delivery practices.
This course examines the application of theatre as a tool to provoke, promote, and produce social change through a variety of methodologies.
Prerequisite Narrative: THETR-100
Notes: Students will work with local or national organizations and individuals to research and address issues of community concern through the creation of collaboratively created theatrical works.

Course Name: Technology in Education: Issues and Opportunities
Course Description: What is the difference between learning from technology and learning with technology? This course explores the role of technology in learning and critically analyzes the cognitive, social, political, and logistical aspects of education technology in the K-12 public school setting. Students will research and develop a learning model incorporating technology in a proposal for a specific grade range in a public school system of the future. Hands-on experiences critically assessing technology in constructivist based learning are required.
Prerequisite Narrative: one full-unit education studies course or permission of instructors.

Course Name: The Local-Global Tug of War: Glocalization of Higher Education
Course Description: In this dynamic course, students will embark on a journey to understand the intricate interplay between globalization and localization within the realm of higher education. Through interdisciplinary exploration, we will examine how higher education institutions grapple with the tension between globalizing trends and local cultural contexts.
