Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy (PHIL) or Africana Studies (AFRST), or consent of instructor

Course Description: This course is a Justice Lab writing workshop in which students will focus on philosophical issues related to communities, violence, and guns. Students will learn to write for a non-specialist audience.

Analysis of the idea of democracy, traditions of democratic theory (liberal, Marxist, elitist) and current problems of democracy in practice. Topics include liberty and equality, community power, participation and bureaucracy.
Exploration of the spiritual power attributed to philosophy by Jewish, Greek, and other philosophers.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy or Classics

Course Description: An introductory survey of philosophical approaches to death and dying. Topics to be discussed include definitions of death, the ‘good death,’ death and identity, whether and when death is a harm, death and suspended vitality, ethics in end-of-life care, posthumous harms, what we owe to the dead, and the possibility of an afterlife.

Twentieth-century and contemporary philosophers often focus on the role of language in philosophical questions, whether to clear up mistaken or misleading uses of language or for its own sake.  This survey course will look at the most important philosophers of language and how they approach questions of reference, meaning, and linguistic ontology, including Frege, Russell, Tarski, Quine, Putnam, Kripke, and Chomsky.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy or consent of instructor

Course Description: Focus on the philosophical analysis of scientific knowledge, scientific method and the practice of science.  Readings include classic texts in the philosophy of science as well as contemporary discussions of science as a social product and critiques of the notion of scientific objectivity.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHIL-203 and either PHIL-120 or PHIL-235, or consent of the instructor

Course Description: A course in comparative philosophy. We will examine, compare, and contrast various philosophers, philosophical systems, and schools of thought from both eastern and western philosophy. For instance, we may examine the philosophies of Sextus Empiricus, the ancient greek (Pyrrhonian) skeptic, and Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school of Mahayana Buddhism; we may draw comparisons between the ancient Roman Stoics and the philosophical life of Mohandas Gandhi; and we may investigate similarities or highlight important differences between the ethical systems of Aristotle and Confucius.
Prerequisite Narrative: Two courses in Philosophy

Course Description: What does writing style have to do with philosophical content? We will look at the "old quarrel" between the philosophers and the poets, and look at the ways in which philosophy was and is written, to think about what counts as philosophy and why and how we mark it off from its others. Readings by Borges, Calvino, Kafka, Coetzee, Plato and others.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy (PHIL), Literature (LIT), Creative Writing (CRWR) or consent of instructor

Course Description: A close examination of the emergence, aims, and argumentative styles of Critical Race Theory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHIL-112 / AFRST-112 or PHIL-115 or consent of instructor

Course Name: Black Joy: Expressions, Practices, and Existential Significance
Course Description: This course explores Black joy as a vital site of creativity, resistance, and existential meaning in the lives of people situated as Black. While much scholarship on Black life focuses on structures of oppression and resistance, this course turns attention to the generative, life-affirming practices of joy that animate Black communities across time and place. From music, dance, and literature to spiritual practices, everyday rituals, and collective celebrations, we will examine how joy functions not simply as fleeting pleasure but as a profound mode of survival, a politics of possibility, and an existential grounding in the face of systemic devaluation.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHIL-115 and one course in AFRST or consent of instructor

Course Description: This course will be a survey of the philosophical literature on the idea and definition of human nature.
Prerequisite Narrative: Two previous courses in philosophy, including at least one of PHIL-120, PHIL-201, PHIL-203, or PHIL-239, or by permission of the instructor.

Course Description:
What is critical consciousness? Why would anyone want to be critically conscious? What are the existential implications of being critically conscious? How does one become critically conscious and what are the habits of those who are critically conscious?

This is a course dedicated to taking up these questions individually and collectively with respect to their relevance personally and socially. Moreover, this is a course in which students theorize and go through the process of developing a form of critical consciousness relative to contemporary matters of race broadly construed.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHIL-112 or PHIL-115, or one course in AFRST, or consent of instructor

Course Description: Examination of Confucian thought and ritual practice from classical times to the present. Emphasis on reading philosophical and ritual texts in translation in order to understand the ways that Confucians understood their place in Chinese society.
Prerequisite Narrative: Relevant coursework in History (HIST), Asian Studies (ASNST) or Religious Studies (RELST), or consent of instructor

Course Description: Virtue ethics emphasizes the goodness or badness of those who act, rather than the rightness or wrongness of particular actions. The virtues are often taken to contribute to individual happiness, or the ability to construct a meaningful life. We will examine virtue ethics as a theory (and as alternative to consequentialism and deontology). We begin with a survey of ancient versions, before exploring new developments and various applications of virtue ethics to contemporary moral problems (abortion, the treatment of non-human animals, climate change, human over-consumption, and technology).
Prerequisite Narrative: Two courses in Philosophy or consent of instructor

Course Name: When Old Debates Were New Again: The Theoretical Origins of Internet Policy
Course Description: This course offers a critical introduction to internet policy through the lens of political theory. It is organized around five main topics: “the wisdom of the multitude” (Jeremy Waldron), civil disobedience, speech, privacy, and surveillance. While technology is always changing, the guiding refrain for the course is that seemingly novel concerns can often be traced back to old debates.
Prerequisite Narrative: One 200-level course in Political Theory or permission of instructor.

Course Description: Examining the ethical, social, and political implications of belief formation and belief change. Much of modern Western epistemology treats belief as an individual matter.  But knowledge doesn’t work like that.  We’re not isolated, we’re connected, and interdependent: our knowledge comes, not from reflection, but from conversations, imitation, and observation.  Beginning with the Cartesian model of belief and knowledge, this course will survey developments from modern to contemporary social epistemology.  Topics may include: arguments for the existence of god and the debate between faith and reason, the epistemology of testimony, conspiracy theories and the production of ignorance, and intellectual virtues and vices.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy (PHIL)

Course Name: What Is Philosophy? A Seminar on Philosophy's Self-Reckoning
Course Description: This seminar takes up one of philosophy's most unsettling questions — what is philosophy itself? — by centering American philosophy as both a prime site of the question's emergence and a focal point for critical efforts to answer it. Beginning with John Dewey's radical argument that philosophy must abandon its self-image as detached spectator and reconnect with the urgencies of social life, the course traces how that demand was taken up and extended by thinkers working within, against, and beyond the American pragmatist tradition. Over the course of the semester, students will be required to develop and defend a position on what philosophy is, knowing that every answer to that question carries a cost.
Prerequisite Narrative: 3 courses in Philosophy or consent of instructor

Course Name: The Politics of A.I.: Algorithms, "Big Data," and "Humans in the Loop"
Course Description: This upper-level seminar is structured around three concepts that are central to the politics of AI: algorithms, "big data," and "humans in the loop." Issues discussed include algorithmic discrimination, the state of consent in the age of "big data," and the psychological toll of content moderation on social media. Explicitly interdisciplinary, a variety of methods and academic backgrounds are welcome. The course is speaking intensive.
Prerequisite Narrative: 200-level course in Government, Computer Science, Philosophy, or Public Policy or instructor consent

Course Description: An advanced study of analytic epistemology. We will explore contemporary debates about the nature of knowledge, evidence, justification, the structure of the mind, and the significance of truth.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in philosophy or permission of the instructor.

Course Description: Is objectivity possible? If it is, is it an epistemic value worth pursuing? How does objectivity relate to the metaphysics of experience and to our ideals of rationality? How does objectivity relate to truth? Readings will draw from traditional philosophers of science, historians and sociologists of science, feminist philosophers of science and other writings in science studies.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or consent of instructor

Course Description: A broad study of themes through Wittgenstein’s work, including the picture-theory, naming, rule-following, meaning, skepticism, and truth.  While our focus will be on Wittgenstein’s work, we will also spend time on his intellectual forebears and those he influenced, including Frege, Russell, Anscombe, Quine, Kripke, and Diamond.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or permission of instructor

Course Description: This course will give you an opportunity to think carefully about progress. We will read about philosophical conceptions of progress in science, morality, prudence, and philosophy. We will examine popular claims about progress: that AI will revolutionize human societies for the better, that gene selection will allow us to create healthier and happier humans, and that experimentation on animals is worth it because of the intellectual progress it results in. We will ask whether moral and philosophical progress is even possible. And, perhaps most importantly, we will ask practical questions about how to contribute to human progress.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in philosophy or permission of the instructor

Course Description: David Foster Wallace’s fiction and non-fiction are often read through a philosophical lens, given his deep immersion in the analytic philosophical tradition. This course examines the extent to which Wallace’s work is appropriately read as philosophy, and the question of what demarcates philosophy from fiction and from literary non-fiction. Not open to students who have taken PHIL-326.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or three courses in Literature (LIT) or Creative Writing (CRWR), or consent of instructor

Course Description: Explores the role of intuition in our reasoning in epistemology, philosophy of mind, mathematics and moral philosophy, and perhaps other areas. We will consider arguments in favor of using intuitions in philosophy, as well as work on the fallibility of intuition, and the recent movement known as experimental philosophy.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or consent of instructor

Course Description: An intensive study of the philosophical dialogues of Plato, exploring interpretive matters, historical settings, philosophical arguments, and dramatic features.  Special attention will be given to the primary texts, and some time and attention will be spent discussing secondary literature.  The course will span every major area of philosophy (including metaphysics, ethics, epistemology, aesthetics, and logic) just as the works of Plato do.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or PHIL-201

Course Description: An examination of literature in philosophy of mind. Focus on questions and issues such as: What is the mind? How is it related to the body? What is its role in personal identity? How do theories of mind relate to our understanding of affective and cognitive phenomena such as the emotions, will and reason?
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy or consent of instructor

Course Description: How much should we care about what happens in our lives? If we care too much, we risk being mired in anxiety and pain, but if we care too little, we seem to lose something central to our humanity. In this seminar we will explore how various philosophical traditions and ages, from East to West, from Ancient to Contemporary, have aimed to resolve this issue through the notion of detachment. We will consider how detachment—in its various forms—can form a central part of a good human life. We also explore critiques of detachment by examining its connections to authenticity and alienation. Examples of traditions to be explored include Stoicism, Epicureanism, Daoism, Buddhism, Existentialism, and Absurdism.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy or consent of the instructor

Course Description: Investigation of philosophical theories of happiness from the ancient Greeks until today including theories of hedonism, eudaimonism, desire satisfaction, life satisfaction, emotional state theory, and existentialism.  Examination of recent literature from psychology concerning the nature and source of happiness, the ability to measure happiness, and the extent to which personal happiness is beyond our control.  Comparison among happiness, well-being, meaning, and how they contribute to a good life.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy or consent of instructor
Notes: Taught as a seminar. Philosophy concentrators or by permission of the instructor.

Course Description: What are we doing when we engage in moral deliberation and discourse? Are we describing facts that exist independently of our attitudes, or merely expressing preferences? This seminar examines the debate over the status of moral norms and judgments, discussing views like moral realism, relativism, and nihilism. Along the way we will also review arguments based on the evolution of moral norms, the psychology underlying moral and social norms, and the phenomenology of moral judgment.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in philosophy, one of which must be in moral philosophy.

Course Description: It makes sense to see morality as adaptive, yet from an evolutionary perspective it’s puzzling that we follow and enforce moral standards even when it is costly for us to do so. This course will critically examine different sorts of evolutionary accounts of morality (e.g. group selection, cultural evolution), with methodological issues in mind.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy or permission of instructor

Course Description: An existential exploration of voice as that which awakens and embodies critical consciousness. Focusing on voice as it emerges and operates within the context of blackness, the course will focus on various black figures and various black expressions of voice as they relate to existential forms of liberation and empowerment. Seminar.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL), one of which must be PHIL-112, PHIL-115, PHIL-222, PHIL-242, or PHIL-319, or consent of instructor

Course Description: A close examination of Nietzsche’s philosophical corpus that focuses on his conception of the good life as it emerges within the context of the critical and positive aspects of his philosophy. Topics include the existential significance of narrative, the nature of knowledge and the philosophical import of Nietzsche’s critical condemnations of metaphysics, religion and morality.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or consent of instructor
Notes: Open to juniors and seniors. Taught as a seminar.

Course Description: Course will focus on Rorty’s work from his early work on philosophy of mind and epistemology through his work on metaphilosophy and politics. We will read not just Rorty’s major works, but also some of his critics, including Charles Taylor, Bjorn Ramberg, Linda Alcoff, and John McDowell.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or consent of the instructor

Course Description: From politics to taste, disagreements are everywhere. We examine the epistemic, moral, and political significance of disagreement: when,if ever, should disagreement force us to revise our own views? Does the existence of moral disagreement have implications for moral objectivity? And how can we coexist with others who disagree with our most basic values? We will also discuss the differences among disagreements in science, aesthetics, and ethics. We’ll also ask whether the persistence of philosophical disagreement should make us pessimistic about the possibility of philosophical knowledge.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or consent of instructor

Course Description: Advanced work aimed at completing a philosophical essay or experiential project on a topic of each student’s interest.  In collaboration with other members of the seminar, each student will frame and explore a philosophical problem.  For a standard project, students will develop an extended thesis-driven essay.  For an experiential project, students will develop sustained engagement with activities that develop or apply philosophical views outside traditional academic structures in a reflective, creative, and rigorous way.  All projects will be presented publicly at the end of the term.
Notes: Course cannot be taken Credit/No Credit

Course Description: The first semester of a year-long sequence (100-205) for pre-med students and other scientists who require a year of physics. Topics include mechanics, fluids and thermodynamics.  Emphasis on applications of physics in medicine and in other sciences. Three hours of lecture and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: Knowledge of algebra and trigonometry
Notes: First Year students need instructors signature to enroll.

Course Description: The second semester of a year-long sequence (100-105) for pre-med students and other scientists who require a year of physics. Topics include electricity, fluids, waves, optics, atomic physics and nuclear physics. Emphasis on applications of physics in medicine and in other sciences.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-100, PHYS-200 or PHYS-190
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory. Knowledge of algebra and trigonometry required.

Course Description: A few basic physics principles can explain many common devices such as car engines, TVs, refrigerators, airplanes and eyeglasses, and some not-so-common devices such as atomic bombs and lasers.   This course qualitatively teaches basic physics concepts with the aim of demystifying technology.  A conceptual introduction to physics where all the examples come from your experience.

A study of two fundamental developments in modern physics — quantum theory and relativity.  Drawing on the quantum mechanics of spin and space-time diagrams, we gain an overview of some of the more thought-provoking aspects of contemporary physics. Breaking from tradition, this is not a historical survey but instead focuses on the fundamental nature of these two developments, as well as the role of observation in modern physical theory.
Notes: Comfort with simple algebra and geometry helpful.

Course Description: This course is a survey of some of the interesting ways in which fine art intersects math and physics. The curriculum consists of six topics in which some juxtaposition of physics and art is present; in some cases physics is relevant to the context of the art, in some case to the content of the art, and in some cases, both. We begin with some of the earliest works of art and proceed chronologically,  including cave paintings and radiocarbon dating, the Archimedes palimpsest and imaging techniques, and the drip paintings of Jackson Pollock  and their connection to chaotic motion and fractals.
Notes: Familiarity with algebra and calculus recommended.

Course Description: A description of the universe, starting with the appearance and organization of the solar system and working outward. Development of the heliocentric view. Observational deduction of properties of stars. Stellar evolution and its relation to pulsars and black holes. Galaxies and the structure and history of the universe.

An exploration of the physics that underlies the production of musical sounds.  Covers issues ranging from the nature of musical sound, units, some physical principles, theory of wave propagation and mode formation, physical mechanisms of how instrument families work and their implications for musical use of those families, acoustics of halls, digital simulations of musical instruments and performance spaces.  Algebra will be used.  Four hours of class/laboratory per week. May count toward a concentration in physics.

The first semester of a sequence of physics courses for students interested in physical sciences, math or engineering. Normally the first course for students who plan to major or minor in physics. Introduction to principles governing the motion of a particle and of systems of particles. Kinematics and dynamics; energy, linear momentum, angular momentum and conservation laws. Introduction to the laws of special relativity.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-113 (may be taken concurrently)
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory. Sophomores and above need instructor’s signature to enroll.

Course Description: The physics of oscillations, waves and fields. Topics include simple harmonic motion, fluids, sound, electric and magnetic fields, light, optics and interference phenomena. Emphasizes the use of calculus as a tool to describe and analyze the physical world.  Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-190 or PHYS-200 and MATH-116 (may be taken concurrently)

Course Description: The first semester of a year-long calculus-based sequence (200-205) for scientists and pre-med students who require a year of physics. Topics include Newtonian mechanics, conservation laws, fluids, kinetic theory and thermodynamics.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-116 or equivalent. Not open to students who have taken PHYS-100 or PHYS-190.
Notes: Three hours of lecture and three hours of laboratory. First Year students need instructor’s signature to enroll.

Course Description: The second semester of a year-long sequence (200-205) for pre-med students and other scientists who require a year of physics. Topics include electricity and magnetism, optics, relativity, atomic physics and nuclear physics.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-100 or PHYS-200
Notes: Three hours of lecture and three hours of laboratory.

Course Description: An introductory study of the rapidly growing field of QuantumComputation. The course starts with a brief introduction to themathematical framework for describing quantum bits (qubits) andquantum gates. Topics will include physical realizations of qubits(with examples from condensed matter and atomic physics) and selectedquantum algorithms.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290 or permission of the instructor
Notes: MATH-224 or familiarity with matrix multiplication is recommended.

Course Name: Nuclear Weapons in World War II
Course Description: World War II has been called "the physicists’ war"; it was perhaps the first global conflict in which physicists played a central role. In this course we examine the scientific paradigms that shaped physicists’ effort to understand fission, the relevant fission processes, and the technical principles that went into construction of the first atomic weapons. We also examine the structural and institutional hierarchies that were present at the time of the war, the social disparities involved in the fabrication of the weapons,  and the decision to deploy two atomic weapons on Japanese cities.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-195 and MATH-216 or permission of instructor

Course Description: A half-credit course introducing Python programming and computational techniques to solve problems that arise in physics and related fields. Students will visualize and analyze data using skills such as plotting, curve fitting, solving equations, and image analysis. The course will emphasize commonly available scientific libraries.
Prerequisite Narrative: Pre-/Co-requisite: PHYS-195 or permission
Notes: This practical course is taught in a lab format.

Course Description: Hands-on introduction to the concepts and devices of electronics. Study of analog and digital circuits, computer architecture, assembler programming and computer interfacing.
Wave-particle duality, the nuclear atom, the development of Schrödinger’s wave mechanics and the quantum theory of atoms.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-195 or PHYS-205, and MATH-116
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

Course Description: Introduction to the mathematical description of the electric and magnetic fields, their sources and their interactions with matter. Exploration of Maxwell’s laws with emphasis on the relationship between the physics and the mathematics needed to describe it.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290
Notes: Normally taken concurrently with PHYS-245. MATH-216 is recommended. Three hours of class.

Course Description: Independent work on a research project under supervision of a faculty member.
Prerequisite Narrative: Consent of instructor
Notes: One-quarter or one-half credit per semester. Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory only. Students may repeat PHYS-298 for credit, but only a maximum of one-half credit of Physics Research can count towards their concentration.

Course Description: Exploration of observational and theoretical topics in cosmological physics. Topics may include evidence for the Hot Big Bang Model of the Universe, background cosmological evolution and dark energy, the cosmic microwave background, primordial nucleosynthesis, growth of large scale structure, as well as evidence and candidates for dark matter.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290

Course Description: A study of mathematical methods and their use in investigating physical systems. Topics may include ordinary differential equations, special functions, Sturm-Liouville theory, partial differential equations, integral transforms, calculus of complex functions, numerical methods, tensor analysis, and group theory.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-224 and either PHYS-295 or MATH-216, or permission of instructor

Course Description: An introduction to the physics and mathematics of space-time geometry including Einstein’s special and general theories of relativity with applications to black holes, gravitational waves, and cosmology.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-216 or permission of instructor

Course Description: An introduction to condensed matter that explores the physics of metals, insulators, semiconductors, and superconductors, with particular attention to structure, thermal properties, energy bands, and electronic properties. The course draws on quantum physics to explain the origin of these properties and addresses experimental methods commonly used to understand material properties.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290

Course Description: Exploration of topics in contemporary physics using the tools of quantum mechanics developed in PHYS-290. Topics may include multi-electron atoms, molecules, solid state physics, lasers and quantum optics, nuclear physics, quantum computing, and particle physics.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290

Course Description: An examination of the assumptions, paradigms, and hierarchies embedded in science and technology. This course will examine evidence pointing to the structure of hierarchies built into and from science and how those structures may result in inequalities for various groups participating in and affected by science and technology. Topics will vary but might include: the objectivity/subjectivity of science; how biases and social structures intersect with equity, diversity, and inclusion in science; and gender and race disparities in STEM fields.
Prerequisite Narrative: Restricted to Chemistry or Physics concentrators or permission of the instructor.

Course Description: A continuation of PHYS/CHEM 348, focused on applying the general material learned in PHYS/CHEM 348 to real life intersections of physics activities and broader society. In addition to an in-depth case study, students will complete projects using their knowledge of social, structural, and institutional hierarchies to improve the Physics Department.
Notes: This is a half credit continuation of PHYS/CHEM 348 into the second half of the semester.

Course Description: Principles of classical mechanics, including oscillations, nonlinear dynamics, dynamics of systems of particles, non-inertial reference frames, Hamilton and Lagrangian mechanics, celestial mechanics, rigid body motion and coupled oscillations.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-295 or consent of instructor

Course Description: An experimental astrophysics course designed to immerse physics majors and astronomy minors in the hands-on techniques and methodologies central to astrophysical research. Students will use telescopes to collect images that will be calibrated into data sets. These data sets will be analyzed to interpret astrophysical phenomena.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290 or permission of instructor

Course Description: Properties of large-scale systems in terms of a statistical treatment of the motions, interactions and energy levels of particles. Basic probability concepts and the principles of statistical mechanics. Explanation of thermal equilibrium, heat, work and the laws of thermodynamics. Application to various physical systems.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290

Course Description: A series of research projects stressing the integration of theory and experiment. Emphasis on scientific writing, formal oral presentations, use of the current physics literature.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-290
Instructor: Charles Collet; Amani Jayakody; Viva Horowitz

Course Description: An exploration of the mathematical tools and foundations of quantum mechanics. Topics include angular momentum, spin, measurement, bound states and perturbation theory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-350

Course Description: Intensive study of Maxwell’s equations in both differential and integral form; electrostatics and electro-dynamics; special relativity; and the transformation of electromagnetic fields. Introduction to electromagnetic waves and dielectric and magnetic materials.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-295 and PHYS-350 or consent of instructor

Course Description: Independent research in collaboration with faculty supervisor. Students will give a series of formal oral presentations about their research and will write a comprehensive thesis.
Notes: Open to senior concentrators or to others with consent of instructor.

Course Description: Independent research in collaboration with faculty supervisor. Students will give a series of formal oral presentations about their research and will write a comprehensive thesis.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-550

Course Description: This is a beginner level course. The course introduces students to the fundamental skills and techniques of the game. Students will learn proper grip, footwork, serving, strokes, rules, and strategies for gameplay.

This is a beginner level course. The course focuses on the basics of swimming. Students will learn how to build swimming proficiency, enhance endurance, and develop water confidence. Students will practice foundational swim strokes (freestyle, backstroke, butterfly) while mastering proper breathing techniques and essential water safety skills (treading water). Students with no prior swim experience will be provided a gradual progression.

This is a beginner level course. The course educates students on the use of all equipment in the fitness center, and on the basics of creating a workout routine. Topics covered will be cardio exercises, gravity exercises, and resistance training using machines and free weights. Students will be encouraged to implement a sound fitness program that promotes awareness of cardiovascular health and strength training.
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PHYED-206.

Course Description: This course is for all experience levels. The course introduces students to the weight room and its equipment. Students will learn the basics of lifting free weights and will work through a progression of programming. Experienced students are encouraged to participate to enhance their fitness journey with advanced programming.

This is a beginner level course. The course introduces students to the fundamentals of the game of golf including the rules, etiquette, and essential mechanics of play. Students will learn and practice basic skills that will enable them to enjoy golf as a lifetime recreational activity.

This is a beginner level course. The course introduces students to cardiovascular exercising through jogging. Students will learn how to monitor their body and the different training zones. Students will explore the various places on campus to jog (Fitness Center, Pritchard Outdoor Track, Margaret Bundy Scott Fieldhouse Indoor track).

This course is for all experience levels. This course helps provide a full-body workout to strengthen muscles and boost cardiovascular fitness through a combination of resistance training, body weight exercises, cardio, and core strength. Students will learn how to create their own full body workout.
This course is for all experience levels. This class will teach the rules and strategies of racquetball through game play. Students will learn different strokes, the serve, and playing strategies.

This is a beginner level course, however all experience levels are welcome. This course covers the fundamentals of top rope (TR) climbing. Students will learn how to select and fit personal climbing equipment, tie-in as a climber, learn TR belay technique, and cover basic climbing movements. Climbers will have a chance to take their belay test to get checked-off to belay at the Hamilton College climbing wall.

This is a beginner level course. Students will learn basic ice skating skills on balance, stride, edge control, and stopping. Students will develop confidence and coordination through a combination of structured drills and free time skate.

This course is for all experience levels. This course introduces the basic shots in squash including drives, volley, and serves. Drills and practice games provide opportunities to apply the basic techniques and tactics of squash.

This course is for all experience levels. This course introduces students to all aspects of tennis. Students will learn the rules, scoring, grip, serves, volleys, returns, stance, groundstrokes, as well as strategies for both singles and doubles play.
This course is for all experience levels. This course introduces the rules, skills and strategies of the game of volleyball. Classes involve skill instruction and daily game play.

This is an intermediate level course. This course provides students visibility into the athletic training profession. This course will provide an overview of the prevention and management of athletic injuries with an emphasis on taping/wrapping procedures. Students will develop skills in maintaining their health via a physically active lifestyle.

This course is for all experience levels. This course is a relaxing and peaceful introduction to the postures of yoga with a focus on alignment and breathwork. Flowing sequences of vinyasa are moderately introduced. Lessons in meditation are offered during every class prior to savasana (rest).

This is an intermediate level course. This course is a dynamic and fast-paced style of yoga that combines strength, flexibility, and breath work in a flowing sequence of poses. Some basic meditation lessons will be included throughout the 12 classes offered.
This is an intermediate level course. The course is for students looking to enhance their swimming skills while learning how to exercise in an aquatic environment to help develop a lifelong practice.

This is for all experience levels. This course introduces the basic skills and rules of basketball. Instruction will focus on the proper fundamentals of shooting, passing, and dribbling. Students will gain new skills and/or refine their technique through drills and practice games.

This course is for all experience levels. The course is for designed for all levels and involves the use of spin bikes to build muscle endurance and cardio fitness. The course includes topics on pace, cadence, resistance, and proper seat heights.

This is a beginner level course. The course is a variation on the game of volleyball and is played in a racquetball court. Students will learn the rules, serving technique, and strategies for game play.
This course is for all experience levels. The course offers a team approach to learning bocce ball. Students will learn the basic rules, strategies, and variations of the game through casual play.

This is a beginner level course. The course will introduce students to the fundamental techniques of indoor target archery focusing on equipment care and usage, range, safety, stance, shooting technique, and scoring methods.
This is a beginner level course. Students will learn the rules, scoring, and strategies of spike ball. The class is taught in the form of team play and offers a fun and supportive environment.

This course is for all experience levels. This course introduces the basic rules, strokes, shots, and strategies of pickleball. Through drills and practice games students will develop basic techniques and strategies of game play.

This course is for all experience levels. The course explores the scenic trails of the Kirkland Glen, Root Glen, and various routes on campus. This course emphasizes stress relief, healthy habits, and an appreciation of nature. Good walking or hiking shoes are highly recommended.

This is a beginner level course. The course explores emotional and physical well-being, self-care, and introspection, among other topics. Students will gain knowledge and learn strategies to support their own mental and physical health, while also promoting wellness and care for others.

This is a beginner level course. The course introduces students to the skills, rules, and techniques of frisbee golf. Students will learn strategies and scoring. The layout of the course includes 9 holes across the softball field. Various formats will be used when playing (scramble, match play) ending with a tournament on the last two days of class.

This is a beginner and intermediate levels course. Students will learn proper rowing machine technique and sequencing (catch, drive, finish, and recovery). Sessions blend steady-state rowing with intervals, body weight exercises, and dynamic stretch. This is a low-impact course.

This is a beginner level course. The course is non-contact. Students will learn basic punching, kicking, footwork, and body-movement techniques.  Self-defense strategies are incorporated. Students will engage in station drills, shadowboxing, calisthenics, striking a bag, and partner work to build strength, fitness, coordination, and confidence.

Course Name: Foundations of Health and Human Practices
Course Description: Foundations of Health and Human Practices is a physical education course focused on developing lifelong habits of wellness through movement, self‑reflection, and mental health awareness. Students explore physical activity, stress management, mindfulness, and personal goal‑setting while examining how physical, mental, and emotional health are interconnected. The course encourages self‑care, resilience, and informed decision‑making to support overall well‑being and healthy living.

This course is for all experience levels. Students will learn the rules and strategies of cornhole. As a popular activity involving teamwork and strategy, students will work together and compete in different game formats.

This is an advanced level course. The course is for students who want to challenge themselves physically and mentally. Faculty will utilize exercises that include running hills, weighted sleds, advanced plyometrics, direction sprint work, and interval training. Prior physical conditioning is strongly recommended to taking this course.

Focus on the American system of law: principally constitutional law, criminal law, and the development of civil rights. Topics include philosophical approaches to justice, English common law, and comparative analysis of French civil law and legal codes in socialist political systems and in majority Muslim countries. Consideration of the challenges to trust in legal institutions from the Supreme Court to local courts and police. Attention also to legal regimes regarding refugees, Native Americans, and defendants with mental illness.

An overview and analysis of US health care systems. US health care systems include public health (population-based services) and medical care (individual patients) systems. Topics include development and organization of various public health and medical entities within the United States, strengths and challenges related to cost, quality, and access to these systems, past and present epidemics, and current issues related to health care systems.
Notes: May not be counted toward the concentration or minor. Not open to students who have taken BIO-216.

Course Name: Bureaucracy and Public Administration: Experts, Elites, and Governance
Course Description: This course examines the institutional role of specialized experts in public administration. Drawing primarily on cases in the United States, it focuses on the historical development, current practices, and ethical implications of bureaucratic governance. What is the role of specialized expertise in solving public problems? How should experts and administrators relate to the mass public? What are the political, policy, and ethical consequences of institutionalizing expertise in bureaucratic agencies? The course will use both contemporary and classic readings from political science and public policy to explore theses questions.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-116

Course Description: Drawing implications from data has become essential to building successful careers. This course guides students through developing a meaningful social science research question and designing an empirical study suitable for investigating their questions. We consider how to conduct transparent, rigorous, and evidence-based research, engage with statistical tools, and learn the basics of R.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-116 or GOVT-251 / PPOL-251
Notes: Not open to students who have taken ECON 266.

Course Description: Introductory survey of topics surrounding asylum in comparative perspective. Analysis of contemporary issues surrounding displacement and humanitarian protections including but not limited to human rights conventions, refugee resettlement and camps, irregular migration, the politicization of refugees, political discourse and securitization, offshore processing, and climate displacement. Case study of refugee producers and hosts such as the United States, the European Union, Venezuela, Syria, Australia, Palestine, Kenya, Turkey, South Korea, and Myanmar.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-112 or GOVT-114

Course Description: What is human happiness?  What factors increase or decrease it?  Why are some countries and cultures happier than others?  How can government policies promote happiness?  This course considers:-- the nature of happiness from the major philosophical traditions, --the cognitive biases that impede our ability to maximize happiness,  --the empirical literature on subjective well-being from the fields of economics, political science, and psychology,  --recent trends in capitalist societies and their effects on happiness, and  --government policies that might improve human happiness.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in statistics, from any discipline.

Course Description: The study of policy analysis using and comparing a variety of disciplinary and analytic traditions.  Consideration of controversies over particular policies at the national and local level and the premises underlying them.   Examination of methods and principles used in formulating and  evaluating public policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-100 or ECON-101
Notes: Open to seniors with consent of instructor. (American Politics)

Course Description: Investigation of health policy from a comparative perspective. The course introduces fundamental concepts in health policy and examines different health care systems across the globe as well as case studies in health care delivery and public health.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-112, GOVT-251 / PPOL-251, or consent of the instructor

Course Name: Utica in the Context of US History
Course Description: Utica, New York, as a case study in US history.  Examines its evolution from early post-Revolutionary "western frontier" settlement to center of industry and technological innovation, to early "rust belt" city and, more recently, to early center of refugee resettlement.  Themes will include:  transportation and communications, industrialization, demographic transformation, religion, politics, ethnic nationalism, labor history, xenophobia and racism, war and conflict, architecture, suburbanization, organized crime, political corruption, Urban Renewal, deindustrialization, urban decay.  Readings and discussions will include relevant primary documents.
This seminar forms part of the justice lab program. It focuses on issues of politics and policy.
Instructor: Heather Sullivan (and others in the gov department)
Notes: This course forms part of the Justice Lab. Students must apply to be a part of the lab.

Course Description: Students will work two 3 hour, half-day periods each week Requires discussion, journaling and a research paper that synthesizes various parts of the Justice Lab.
Corequisite Narrative: Part of the integrated, 4 course Justice Lab.
Notes: Must be taken concurrently with other Justice Lab courses. Retakeable for a maximum of two times.

Course Name: Inspired Action: Religion, Spirituality and Community Building
Course Description: Religious and spiritual communities have long been involved in building community and supporting people who are marginalized and lack sufficient resources. In this class, with input from community partners, students will learn about how religion and spirituality can be mobilized into civic action. When possible, this course will include experiential learning and involve doing collaborative work with and for community partners.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in SOC or PPOL

Course Description: Introduces theories and practices that focus on repairing harm caused by criminal or personal injury. We will examine various processes, involving both the injured party and perpetrator, which acknowledge the truth of the injustice endured, and — suspending the punitive repercussions of the violation — focus on the interpersonal work of reparations and mutual understanding of the damage done, and possibilities for healing and reconciliation. We will examine the work of Buber, Zehr, and Tutu/ Mandela in their role with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, as well as a similar commission established in Canada to address the violation of Indigenous children in residential schools. We will explore the roots of restorative justice in moral philosophy and biblical and other sacred texts.
Notes: This course will engage case studies and projects on and off campus to explore practical applications of restorative justice.

Course Name: Religion and Immigration in Central New York
Course Description: This course will take advantage of our location in Central New York to provide a geographical and historical approach to the varieties of religious experiences in the land we now call the United States, highlighting the role that immigration has played through history. The first half of the course will center on the Erie Canal, examining the many ways the canal remade religious life in the US in the 19th century. The second half of the course will jump ahead to post-1965 life in the US and the role of immigration on contemporary religious life, with special attention to the city of Utica. Infrastructure, and material-based realities of socio-political life will be stressed. The course will include site visits and a required service learning component.
Corequisite Narrative: Participation in the Justice Lab program
Notes: The course is designed to be part of the Utica Justice Lab for the Spring of 2023.

Course Description: This course examines conflict from a variety of perspectives. We will investigate how arbitration, adjudication, and mediation differ, in addition to exploring how the policies and strategies of cultural and legal institutions dictate different approaches to mediation. Societies cope with conflict by enacting policies consistent with their culture and values. This course examines conflict resolution policies in the U.S. and abroad, including the legal system, the media, the educational sector, and international dispute resolution.
Prerequisite Narrative: COMM-101, COMM-103, COMM-106, COMM-230, or consent of instructor

Course Description: This course provides an introduction to microeconomic analysis and its applications to environmental policy. We first consider the conditions under which markets fail to efficiently allocate scarce resources in the context of environmental issues, such as managing natural resources and climate change. We examine policy instruments including regulations, taxes, subsidies, quotas, and tradable permits to address those market failures. The last part of the course focuses on analyzing distributive impacts of environmental policies and understanding the economic forces behind environmental justice issues.
Prerequisite Narrative: ECON-100

Course Name: The Politics of Global Prison Reform
Course Description: Why does prison reform occur and when does it work? This class explores the politics of prison reform throughout the globe. We will explore cases in which carceral policies shifted in a more punitive direction as well as cases in which reforms attempted to create safer, less crowded, and more humane prisons. We will examine the ways that state actors facilitate or hinder the implementation of prison policies. And, given the course's global focus, will also explore how non state actors like gangs influence the politics of reform and its implementation.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-112 or GOVT-114 or GOVT/PPOL 251

Course Name: Justice Lab Practicum: The Crisis of Youth Gun Violence
Course Description: This practicum involves students directly in the process of law enforcement and criminal justice reform organized by an independent group in Oneida County: Colleges and Community for Unity and Change. The practicum is offered in conjunction with a similar course taught at Utica College. Hamilton students will deploy and analyze a survey of residents of the County, organize focus groups, canvas community organizations, and present proposals for best- practice demonstration projects. Students will develop skills useful to evaluating and reforming criminal justice institutions in other settings.

This course focuses on understanding community-mobilization, organizational leadership models and perspectives for creating social change. It will promote an intersectional understanding of campus and community conditions that give rise to damaging experiences. Students will collaboratively develop leadership change strategies that oppose more common, “expert”-driven approaches.
Prerequisite Narrative: Prerequisite: Participation in LLI  (January), Intro-level course in WMGST, PPOL, AFRST, or SOC or consent of the instructor.
Notes: SSIH with consent of department.  Required field study: week one of spring break.

Course Description: This course helps students understand what public policy analysis is, provides them with a toolkit of practical methods for analysis, and emphasizes professional communication of results in writing. Specifically, it introduces students to cost-benefit analysis and natural-experimental approaches for policy evaluation with real-world examples.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-230 and ECON-166

Course Description: How does people's decision-making process affect public policy and management outcomes? Policymakers, policy analysts, managers, front-line workers, and citizens are all important decision makers. This course draws on scholarship from behavioral economics, psychology, and management, and considers how one might apply these insights in the design and implementation of policies.
Prerequisite Narrative: GOVT-251 or PPOL-251

Course Name: The Politics of A.I.: Algorithms, "Big Data," and "Humans in the Loop"
Course Description: This upper-level seminar is structured around three concepts that are central to the politics of AI: algorithms, "big data," and "humans in the loop." Issues discussed include algorithmic discrimination, the state of consent in the age of "big data," and the psychological toll of content moderation on social media. Explicitly interdisciplinary, a variety of methods and academic backgrounds are welcome. The course is speaking intensive.
Prerequisite Narrative: 200-level course in Government, Computer Science, Philosophy, or Public Policy or instructor consent

Course Description: Examination of program evaluation as a sound methodology for assessing the quality of proposed government interventions and for judging the success or failure of initiatives.  We will explore theory, techniques, and tools to design high-impact programs.  Best practices and cases will be employed to assist class participants as they explore solutions to vexing social problems.  Students will ultimately build their own proposed program using the Bloomberg iTeams approach.
Prerequisite Narrative: Consent of Department

Course Description: A one semester senior project, culminating in a public policy analysis. This is the capstone course in the Public Policy concentration.

Orients students to the concepts, processes and scientific principles of behavior on which the field of applied behavior analysis was founded. Topics of study will include the history and defining features of applied behavior analysis as well as the role of basic principles in producing socially meaningful behavior change (positive and negative reinforcement, punishment, discriminative control of behavior and motivating operations).
Prerequisite Narrative: Psych/Neuro 201 if the course is to count toward the concentration or minor.
Notes: Open only to participants in the Cooperative Educational Program at the New England Center for Children.

Course Name: Behavioral Assessment for Children with Special Needs
Course Description: An introduction to key concepts, methods and ethical considerations associated with behavioral assessment. Objectives will include teaching students to distinguish between idiographic and norm-referenced assessment approaches, to conduct pertinent behavioral assessments (preference assessments, functional assessments and skills assessments), and to incorporate assessment outcomes with treatment selection and design in accordance with contemporary best practices in the field of applied behavior analysis.
Prerequisite Narrative: Psych/Neuro 201 if the course is to count toward the concentration or minor.
Notes: Open only to participants in the Cooperative Educational Program at the New England Center for Children.

Course Description: This course will prepare students to identify, implement, and maintain effective behavioral interventions in applied settings. Specific objectives will include teaching students to select and implement function-based interventions for the reduction of problem behaviors, skills-based prevention strategies, and a variety of behavioral teaching tactics. Tactics for promoting procedural integrity and facilitating the generalization and maintenance of treatment effects will also be reviewed.
Prerequisite Narrative: Psych/Neuro 201 if the course is to count toward the concentration or minor.
Notes: Open only to participants in the Cooperative Educational Program at the New England Center for Children.

Course Description: Equips students with skills needed to confirm the clinical efficacy of interventions by subjecting them to experimental evaluation using single-subject designs. Students will learn to develop valid and reliable systems for measuring behavior, to display data using popular and accessible graphing software, and to assess for orderly changes in behavior through visual inspection and interpretation of graphic data.
Prerequisite Narrative: Psych/Neuro 201 if the course is to count toward the concentration or minor.
Notes: Open only to participants in the Cooperative Educational Program at the New England Center for Children.

Course Description: Provides students with a comprehensive review of empirically supported behavioral teaching procedures for individuals with autism and related disabilities. Topics will focus on teaching skills in a variety of content areas such as language, social, and self-help. Procedures for teaching these include, match-to-sample discrimination training, task analysis, as well as prompting procedures including prompt fading and video modeling.
Prerequisite Narrative: Psych/Neuro 201 if the course is to count toward the concentration or minor.
Notes: Open only to participants in the Cooperative Educational Program at the New England Center for Children.

Course Description: An introduction to the science of human behavior. Topics include the nervous system, perception, learning, motivation, cognitive and social development, personality, individual differences, social behavior and psychopathology. In class laboratory exercises to emphasize the use of research methods and data to describe and examine behavior.
Notes: Some sections may be offered as First-Year Courses.

Course Name: Thriving in the Classroom and Beyond
Course Description: In this first-year course, we will explore lessons from psychology on how to optimize the college experience. Students will discover the science behind academic success and personal well-being as we discuss topics such as self-control, learning and memory, identity formation, belonging, relationships, and stress. Through reflection and regular practice of techniques for managing time, focus, and emotions, this course will help students “know thyself” and find ways to thrive during their time on the Hill.

Course Name: Cognitive Neuroscience in Film, Art, and Media
Course Description: Filmmakers and artists have long used the intricacies of the mind as source material for compelling explorations of the human condition. Through activities, reflections, and discussion, students in this course will examine the psychological and neural underpinnings of such creative endeavors. We will use examples from film, art, and media to critically consider topics such as the difference between the world we sense and the world we perceive; the role of mechanisms such as attention, learning, and decision-making in crafting our narratives; and the benefits and pitfalls of being influenced by perceptual and social patterns in our environment.
Collaborative research under the supervision of a faculty member. Focus on data collection and/or analysis.  Three to four hours per week of lab work.
Prerequisite Narrative: Permission of the instructor.
Notes: Student performance will be evaluated as Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory. One-quarter credit per semester. May be repeated for credit, but does not count toward concentration requirements.

Course Name: Statistics and Research Methods in Psychology
Course Description: The application and interpretation of descriptive and inferential statistics in the study of psychological processes. Some instruction in research design and methodological issues. Students will learn to use the statistical computer program SPSS to analyze data. Topics include the principles of hypothesis testing, t tests, analysis of variance, regression, and some non-parametric statistics.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-101; PSYCH-105; or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109

Course Description: Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a behavioral and cognitive perspective. Survey of experimental and clinical research involving humans and non-human animals, addressing presumed neural mechanisms for cognitive, motivational and emotional states. Analysis of amnesia, aphasia, agnosias, apraxias and disconnection syndromes.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-101, PSYCH-105, or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109

Course Description: Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a biological perspective. In-depth examination of fundamental concepts in neurobiology designed to introduce students to the electrophysiological, chemical and anatomical features of neurons, brain regions and brain circuits. Investigation of the neurobiological basis of behavior through exploration of topics such as neuronal communication, neuroanatomy, sensory and motor systems, learning, motivation, and behavior disorders.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-101; PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109; or any BIO-100

Course Description: An overview of the theoretical orientations, treatment approaches and empirical literature in the field of counseling psychology. Examines the mechanisms by which counseling interventions facilitate personal and interpersonal functioning with a focus on emotional, social, educational, vocational and developmental concerns.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-101; PSYCH-105; or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109
Notes: Does not count toward the Psychology or Neuroscience concentration or the Psychology minor.

Course Name: Psychological Bias in the Justice System
Course Description: How does group membership (e.g., sex, race, mental health status) shape one's experiences with the criminal justice system? Adopting a chronological approach through an exemplar criminal case (e.g., arrest, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, sentencing, release), this course will use case law and empirical research to explore the law's continuing efforts - and shortcomings - in addressing and decreasing bias. Does not count toward the Psychology or Neuroscience concentration or the Psychology minor.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-101, PSYCH-105, or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PSYCH 367.

Course Description: Collaborative research under the supervision of a faculty member. Focus on data collection and/or analysis. Six to eight hours per week of lab work, plus final oral presentation or research paper.
Prerequisite Narrative: Permission of the instructor
Notes: Student performance will be evaluated as Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory. One-half credit per semester. May be repeated for credit, but does not count toward concentration requirements.

Course Description: Theoretical and methodological examination of the study of moral psychology. Topics include moral development, moral emotions, political/cultural differences, moral judgment and behavior, and cooperation. Class time will be devoted to discussion of theoretical and empirical research articles. Laboratory component involves conducting two research projects. Data collection, statistical analysis, papers based on findings, oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: Theoretical and methodological understanding of the study of the self in social psychology. Topics include organization of self-concept and its effect on information processing; self-awareness; self-esteem maintenance processes; cultural influences; stigmas; and self-regulation. Class time devoted to discussion of research articles. Laboratory component involves conducting two research projects. Data collection, statistical analysis, papers based on findings, oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: Theoretical and methodological examination of the psychological processes involved in regulating thoughts, behavior, and emotions. Emphasis on childhood and adolescence. Questions covered will include: What is executive function and how does it develop? What are the consequences of low or delayed self-control abilities across the lifespan? How can we improve self-control? Data collection, statistical analysis, papers based on findings, oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: An exploration of theoretical and methodological questions involved in the study of learning and neural plasticity. Questions covered will include: What is learning? What are the mechanisms that support neural plasticity, and how do they contribute to learning-induced changes in behavior? How does learning change across the lifespan? Laboratory exercises will include the development of original experiments to elicit and measure learning at the behavioral and neural levels, as well as the analysis of neural data. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201 and PSYCH-204 / NEURO-204 or PSYCH-205 / NEURO-205
Prerequisites: PSYCH-201, , NEURO-201, , PSYCH-204, , NEURO-204, , PSYCH-205, , NEURO-205,
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

Course Description: Theoretical and methodological examination of how leadership potential is socially constructed, evaluated, and rewarded, and how these processes are shaped by gender stereotypes. Topics include leadership prototypes, role congruity and lack-of-fit models, backlash and bias, intersectionality, and the effects of gender and race on leadership evaluations. Class time is devoted to in-depth analysis of research articles and case studies, along with student-led discussions and presentations. Laboratory component involves two original research projects with data collection, statistical analysis, scholarly writing, and oral presentations.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201/ NEURO-201
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory work.

Course Description: Theoretical and methodological examination of the study of human behavior in legal contexts. Topics include psychology of criminal behavior; persuasion in the courtroom; risk assessment and punishment; and the influence of extralegal variables (e.g., race). Class time devoted to critical analysis and discussion of legal cases and psychology research articles. Laboratory component involves conducting two research projects. Data collection, statistical analysis, papers based on findings, oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201 or permission of the instructor

Course Description: Study of brain processes involved in cognition, with a focus on current research designs and techniques. Class discussions will focus on primary research articles covering perception, attention, memory and language systems. Laboratory exercises will include the analysis of structural brain scans and electroencephalographic data, and the design, programming and presentation of original experiments. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201 and PSYCH-204 / NEURO-204 or PSYCH-205 / NEURO-205
Prerequisites: PSYCH-201, , NEURO-201, , PSYCH-204, , NEURO-204, , PSYCH-205, , NEURO-205,
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

Course Description: A theoretical and methodological exploration of the psychological and physiological mechanisms of stress. Questions will include: How does psychological stress impact health and well-being? What neurobiological mechanisms are involved? What is the role of environmental context? Laboratory exercises will include designing original experiments to examine the role of stress on behavior and physiological activity, as well as analyzing data, writing papers based on findings, and oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201 and PSYCH-204 / NEURO-204 or PSYCH-205 / NEURO-205
Prerequisites: PSYCH-201, , NEURO-201, , PSYCH-204, , NEURO-204, , PSYCH-205, , NEURO-205,
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology. (Same as PSYCH-329, NEURO-329.)

Course Description: The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: Take BIO-205 / NEURO-205 / PSYCH-205
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

Course Description: An exploration of theoretical and empirical research on the psychology of friendship, with an emphasis on sociocultural and evolutionary approaches. We will consider questions such as: What is friendship, and what functions does it serve in our lives? How do we seek and maintain friendships? In what ways is friendship similar and different across cultures? Through activities and reflections, students will use course material as a lens for examining their own important relationships.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 or NEURO-201

Course Description: An exploration of sensory systems and perceptual experiences. This course will address how we obtain information from our physical environment and use it to create the vibrant experience of our own bodies and the world around us. An emphasis on vision, but also covering audition, somatosensation, olfaction and gustation. Topics will include methodological approaches, sensory pathways and neurobiological mechanisms, disorders, illusions and multi-sensory interactions.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: This course will explore the interactive relationships among evolved adaptations, development, learning, and culture, emphasizing ways in which these work together to shape individuals’ behavior. Questions covered will include: What does it mean to take an evolutionary approach to psychology? What are the major evolutionary theories, and how have they been used to explain human behavior? What are the methods and assumptions of evolutionary approaches?
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: Introduction to the study of mental disorders in adults, including historical and cultural perspectives. Focus on classification, diagnostic assessment, etiology, treatment, and evaluation of treatment efficacy for the major disorders including anxiety, affective, thought, substance, and eating disorders. Research methods in clinical psychology emphasized. Discussion will include how gender, race, ethnicity, culture, sexuality, and social class relate to our understanding of mental illness and its treatment.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: This course is centered on understanding the neurobiology of the "addicted brain." Strong emphasis on the neurobiological effects of drugs of abuse, including short and longer-term changes in the brain and body that occur in response to drug use and abuse. A sampling of drugs to be discussed include cocaine, heroin, marijuana, hallucinogens and alcohol. Effectiveness of various treatment strategies will also be considered. Some discussion of the social, political and philosophical aspects of addiction to drug and non-drug substances (e.g., food compulsions and pathological gambling).
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: A survey of social psychology, the study of how and why people behave, think, and feel in social situations. Topics include social cognition, stereotyping and prejudice, the self, social influence, attitudes and persuasion, attraction and relationships, aggression, and helping behavior. Emphasis on experimental research methodology.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: An examination of theoretical and empirical research on the creation and structure of memories. Consideration of both theoretical and applied topics within the memory literature, including autobiographical memories, unconscious memories, factors contributing to forgetting, the organization of memories, eyewitness memory, and false memories.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: In this course we will take a social psychological approach to understanding stereotypes, prejudice(s), and discrimination based on race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and other group memberships. We will examine classic and contemporary theories and research on topics such as cognitive, motivational, evolutionary, and sociocultural explanations of prejudice; modern forms of prejudice/implicit bias; the impact of prejudice and discrimination on targets of prejudice; and prejudice reduction.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: This course is an in-depth study of methodologies used in clinical psychology research and practice to assess differences among individuals in personality, neuropsychological functioning, intelligence/aptitude, achievement, and forensic issues. Discussion will include the qualities of a good test, how tests are used in current research, as well as limitations and ethical issues involved in clinical assessment.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Name: Psychological Bias in the Justice System
Course Description: How does group membership (e.g., sex, race, ethnicity, religion) shape one’s experiences with the criminal justice system? Adopting a chronological approach through an exemplar criminal case (e.g., arrest, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, sentencing, release), this course will use case law and empirical research to explore the law’s continuing efforts—and shortcomings—in addressing and decreasing bias.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PSYCH 267.

Course Description: A study of how interactions between mind, body, and society contribute to stress and resilience. In this class we will examine the interplay between various neurobiological, psychological, social, and environmental factors that contribute to individual differences in stress reactivity, recovery, and resilience. An emphasis will be placed on using insights gained from neuroscientific and psychological research to inform the development of interventions and policies. Students will reflect upon their own coping strategies and mental health policy stances through activities and written assignments.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201, NEURO-201 and PSYCH-204, NEURO-204 OR PSYCH-205, NEURO-205
Prerequisites: PSYCH-201, , NEURO-201, , PSYCH-204, , NEURO-204, , PSYCH-205, , NEURO-205,

Course Description: Everyone experiences emotions, but how we define them and measure their impact on daily life is a question that psychologists are still working on today. In this course, we will explore how emotions shape behavior, cognition, interpersonal relationships, and biology. Questions covered will include: What would life be like without emotions? Are emotions experienced similarly across cultures? Do nonhuman animals have emotions? How do emotions affect health?
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: An overview of how interactions between mind and body contribute to health and well-being. Health psychologists investigate how to promote health, as well as how to prevent, cope with, and recover from illness. In this class, we will examine the interplay between various psychological, social, and environmental factors as they relate to general health outcomes and specific diseases. Topics include stress management, social relationships, personality traits, placebo effects, and behavioral changes such as eating, sleep habits, exercise, and drug use.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: In this course we will examine the social influences that drive our attitudes and behaviors. We will explore different models of persuasion, cognitive dissonance, conformity, compliance, obedience, and the group processes that affect our attitudes and behaviors in everyday life. Emphasis on empirical research.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PSYCH-356

Course Description: An introduction to the science of lifespan development, from conception and prenatal development to older age and death. Focuses on multiple domains of development, including cognitive, social, physical, and emotional, with emphasis on how development in all domains is shaped by both biological and social/cultural influences (e.g., gender norms, social class, stereotyping and prejudice).
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: Advanced study of psychological research methods, with a focus on critically evaluating original research, independently designing and executing studies, and writing scientific research reports. Topics include reliability and validity, experimental and non-experimental methods, and effective design of studies.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201

Course Description: An advanced seminar integrating psychological services with immersive field experience. Students complete eight to ten hours per week in a cooperating local agency or school while participating in a structured seminar examining the theoretical foundations of their applied work. The course emphasizes the provision of psychological, educational, and applied behavioral services, with focused attention on methodological rigor, ethical decision-making, and professional practice in psychotherapy, counseling, and educational psychology. Students complete an extensive written project focused on using psychological research to address real world problems at their site.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Psychology and departmental permission
